High-dimensional quantum Schur transforms

Adam Burchardt1,2 , Jiani Fei3 , Dmitry Grinko1,4,5 , Martin Larocca6 , Maris Ozols1,4,5 , Sydney Timmerman3 and Vladyslav Visnevskyi1,7 1QuSoft, Amsterdam 2Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica, Amsterdam 3Stanford Institute for Theoretical Physics, Stanford University 4Institute for Logic, Language and Computation, University of Amsterdam 5Korteweg-de Vries Institute for Mathematics, University of Amsterdam 6Theoretical Division, Los Alamos National Laboratory 7Institute of Physics, University of Amsterdam Email address: adam.burchardt.uam@gmail.com Email address: jianif@stanford.edu Email address: grinko.dimitry@gmail.com Email address: laroccamartin@gmail.com Email address: marozols@gmail.com Email address: sydneyt@stanford.edu Email address: vladislav.visnevskyy@gmail.com
Abstract.

The quantum Schur transform has become a foundational quantum algorithm, yet even after two decades since the seminal 2005 paper by Bacon, Chuang, and Harrow (BCH), some aspects of the transform remain insufficiently understood. Moreover, an alternative approach proposed by Krovi in 2018 was recently found to contain a crucial error. In this paper, we present a corrected version of Krovi’s algorithm along with a detailed treatment of the high-dimensional version of the BCH Schur transform. This high-dimensional focus makes the two versions of the transform practical for regimes where the number of qudits nn is smaller than the local dimension dd, with Krovi’s algorithm scaling as O~​(n4)\widetilde{O}(n^{4}) and BCH as O~​(min⁡(n5,n​d4))\widetilde{O}(\min(n^{5},nd^{4})). Our work addresses a key gap in the literature, strengthening the algorithmic foundations of a wide range of results that rely on Schur–Weyl duality in quantum information theory and quantum computation.

1. Introduction

1.1. Background

The Schur–Weyl duality is a classic and fundamental result in representation theory. From an algebraic perspective, it is a theorem about two subalgebras of the full matrix algebra, one generated by the unitary group and another by the symmetric group. Specifically, Schur–Weyl duality says that the diagonal action of the unitary group Ud\mathrm{U}_{d} on the tensor space ℋ:=(ℂd)⊗n\mathcal{H}\vcentcolon=(\mathbb{C}^{d})^{\otimes n} generates a matrix algebra that is the centralizer of the matrix algebra generated by the tensor representation of the symmetric group Sn\S_{n}, and vice versa. In this sense, Schur–Weyl duality is a consequence of the double centralizer theorem [Eti+11].

However, from a representation-theoretic perspective the Schur–Weyl duality presents a much deeper argument about relating finite-dimensional irreducible representations (irreps) of the unitary and the symmetric groups. In particular, it claims that the tensor space ℋ\mathcal{H} decomposes into a direct sum of tensor products, each formed between a pair of irreducible modules: one of the unitary group and one of the symmetric group. Each such pair carries a shared irrep label, thus relating the irreps of the two groups.

Any basis in which the tensor space ℋ\mathcal{H} decomposes into such a direct sum over tensor products of irreducible modules of the unitary and symmetric groups is called a Schur basis, and any unitary transformation from the standard computational basis to such basis is called a Schur transform.

One notable consequence of the decomposition in a Schur basis is that the symmetric group and the unitary group act on different modules, and thus on different registers in the tensor product pairs. This separation makes Schur transform a powerful tool for quantum algorithms and protocols that exploit either permutation or unitary symmetries, and is precisely the reason why it has found so many applications in quantum information and quantum computing [Har05, Wri16, Bot17].

1.2. Applications

A fundamental problem in quantum information theory is operationally estimating a quantum state, assuming access to identical copies of its density matrix. This naturally fits into the Schur–Weyl duality framework. To exemplify, first, performing weak Schur sampling, i.e. a measurement of the irrep label, can reveal the spectral information of the state, based on a quantum analogue of typical sequences [Har05]. Instances include spectrum estimation [KW01, CM04], quantum property testing [MW18, OW21, SW22], entropy estimation [AISW20], and an approach to the non-abelian hidden subgroup problem [CHW07]. Second, optimal protocols for full state tomography [Key06, HHJWY17, OW16, OW17, HCTMT24] rely on strong Schur sampling, i.e. measuring one of the irrep registers in a particular basis. Third, in the context of quantum state discrimination, the asymptotic error exponents of quantum hypothesis testing [Che+24] are quantified by quantum Stein’s lemma [Hay97, Hay02], quantum Chernoff bound [Aud+07] and quantum Sanov’s theorem [Nöt14, Hay24]. These minimum error probabilities can be expressed by entropic quantities and attained algorithmically by strong Schur sampling with measurement operators based on semi-definite programs [Che+24], pretty-good measurement [Che+24] or representation-theoretical arguments [Hay97, Hay02, Nöt14, Hay24].

Besides state characterization, strong Schur sampling can be used to compute expectation values Tr⁡(O​ρ)\Tr(O\rho) of permutation-invariant observables OO or permutation operators OO. Virtual cooling [Cot+19] and virtual distillation for error mitigation [Hug+21] are applications in this spirit. Nevertheless, in specific cases, such as the moment Tr⁡(O​σ⊗n)\Tr(O\sigma^{\otimes n}) where OO is a cyclic shift and σ\sigma a single-qudit state, the expectation can be computed much more efficiently by adding an ancilla and using the generalized swap test, see [HE02, SCC19] and in particular [Bru04].

In the remainder of this subsection we discuss applications to quantum machines, i.e. subroutines with quantum outputs, rather than sampling tasks. A prominent class of examples are unitarily covariant quantum channels, including those for universal compression [Sch95, JHHH98, HM02, HM03, YCH16], entanglement distillation [MH07, BCG14], optimal pure state cloning [GM97, KW99, Har13], purification of mixed states [CEM99, KW01a, LFIC24, Chi+25], and quantum majority vote [BLMMO22]. A common first step to all of these protocols is weak Schur sampling followed by holding the post-measurement state in the Schur basis.

Since we improve the gate complexity for high-dimensional quantum Schur transform, the last two classes of examples concern this regime. Quantum simulation of identical particles is a subfield where quantum Schur transforms become indispensable. Two bases of Hilbert spaces are often considered. The first one is the spin-orbital basis in first quantization [Bas+25, BGMT17] (resp. the occupation basis in second quantization [BF25]), in cases where a Hamiltonian is sparse in it. Any fermionic or bosonic state can then be prepared by an inverse quantum Schur transform (resp. quantum Paldus transform [BF25]), applied to a state in the totally antisymmetric or symmetric sector in the total spin basis (resp. in any sector of the UGA basis [BF25]). The second one is the irrep-decomposing basis, in cases where a Hamiltonian possesses favorable symmetries [BF25, GSŞ21, LRS23, AMR19]. The whole simulation is then sandwiched by a pair of quantum Schur transforms (resp. quantum Paldus transforms) and guaranteed to be efficient, called fast-forwarding.

The optimal measurement in port-based teleportation (PBT) is highly symmetric and thus most conveniently expressed in Schur basis. It was recently shown that PBT can be implemented in time O~​(n​d4)\widetilde{O}(nd^{4}) [GBO23a, GBO23]. By first compressing the alphabet down to nn, our Schur circuit removes the d4d^{4} dependence, yielding a runtime O~​(n4)\widetilde{O}(n^{4}), which is dominated by Krovi’s transform. Complexities of PBT protocols [FTH23] which directly use Schur transform as a subroutine are also improved accordingly.

Finally, variational quantum algorithms [ZLLSK23] and quantum machine learning [Rag+23, SLNSC24, ZLSKL25, Lar+22, Ngu+24] also take advantage of the quantum Schur transform.

1.3. Prior work and our objective

The seminal and first efficient quantum circuits for the quantum Schur transform were constructed by Bacon, Chuang, Harrow (BCH) in [Har05, BCH06]. The circuits use an iterative list of Clebsch–Gordan transforms of the unitary group Ud\mathrm{U}_{d}, each of which couples one tensor factor of the tensor space to the irreps of Ud\mathrm{U}_{d} decomposing the preceding, say, ii factors, and decompose these tensor products into irreps in the i+1i+1 factors. The circuits have a time complexity of poly⁡(n,d,log⁡ϵ−1)\poly(n,d,\log\epsilon^{-1}) for accuracy ε\varepsilon. Recently this complexity was refined to O~​(d4​n)\widetilde{O}(d^{4}n)11 1 In the sequel, we will hide the generic poly⁡(log⁡ϵ−1)\poly(\log\epsilon^{-1}) factors in complexity analyses, which come from compilations of numeric quantum gates that can be obtained using the Solovay–Kitaev theorem. by [Ngu+24].

Krovi enriched the collection by presenting an algorithm for the Schur transform [Kro19] whose framework is the representation theory of the symmetric group Sn\S_{n}, compared to Ud\mathrm{U}_{d} in BCH. In particular, representations of Sn\S_{n} induced from a certain subgroup of Sn\S_{n}, called the Young subgroup, are decomposed into irreps using the quantum Fourier transform over Sn\S_{n} as a subroutine. The time complexity was claimed to be poly⁡(n,log⁡d)\poly(n,\log d). The noteworthy logarithmic factor of dd came from compressing the type vectors in the preparation step, following a description in the footnote in Section 8.1.2 of [Har05].

The objective of the current paper is two-fold. First, Krovi’s paper [Kro19] was recently found [FTH24] to contain a crucial error in its final step. We address and correct it. Second, we work out the detailed circuit of the mentioned compression. Because it puts the subsequent operations on nn instead of dd wires, it should only be included when the local dimension dd is greater than the number of qudits nn. Consequentially, we construct high-dimensional BCH and Krovi circuits, and perform in-depth analyses of their gate, time, and space complexities.

Other efficient quantum algorithms for the Schur transform include [KS18] and [WS24]. Recently, the Schur transform was generalized to tensors of mixed unitary symmetry, whose dual is, in analogy to the symmetric group, the partially transposed permutation matrix algebra. The corresponding basis change can also be efficiently implemented [GBO23a, Ngu23, Gri25]. Streaming versions of the Schur and mixed Schur transforms can be found in [CM23, CMT24].

1.4. Main results

1.4.1. Revised Krovi approach

Krovi’s last step was erroneous in that although it accurately claimed that the copies of each distinct Sn\S_{n} irrep that decompose a target induced representation were labeled by Gelfand–Tsetlin (GT) patterns, it didn’t really transform to this multiplicity space basis from one labeled by standard Young tableaux (SYT), which was a remnant of applying the Sn\S_{n} Fourier transforms.

We first identify this change of basis block-diagonally as one from a split basis of an Sn\S_{n} irrep λ\lambda, i.e. subgroup-reduced down a tower Sn⊃Sμ1+⋯+μl−1×Sμl⊃⋯⊃Sμ1×Sμ2×⋯×Sμl=Yμ\S_{n}\supset\S_{\mu_{1}+\cdots+\mu_{l-1}}\times\S_{\mu_{l}}\supset\cdots\supset\S_{\mu_{1}}\times\S_{\mu_{2}}\times\cdots\times\S_{\mu_{l}}=Y_{\mu}, to the standard basis, i.e. down the tower Sn⊃Sn−1⊃⋯⊃S1\S_{n}\supset\S_{n-1}\supset\cdots\supset\S_{1}. Computing the entries of this entire block is neither practical, because of the generically highly degenerate branching down each level of the tower for the split basis, nor necessary. All we need is a submatrix, an isometry Vλ,μV_{\lambda,\mu} mapped from the trivial sector of the split basis. Each basis element in this sector can be labeled by a multiplicity-free chain of irreps λ⊃(λl−1,(μl))⊃⋯⊃((μ1),…,(μl))=triv\lambda\supset(\lambda_{l-1},(\mu_{l}))\supset\cdots\supset((\mu_{1}),\dots,(\mu_{l}))=\mathrm{triv}, a GT pattern, or a semistandard Young tableau (SSYT).

Our representation theoretic results therefore include, a formula for each matrix entry of each isometry Vλ,μV_{\lambda,\mu}, and a rigorous proof that appending Vλ,μ†V^{\dagger}_{\lambda,\mu} to the Krovi circuit results in the Gelfand–Tsetlin bases for both Sn\S_{n} and Ud\mathrm{U}_{d}. The strategies are deeply rooted in the Schur–Weyl duality: when embedded in the tensor space, the basis transformation Vλ,μV_{\lambda,\mu} of the Sn\S_{n} irrep λ\lambda occurs in the multiplicity space of its Ud\mathrm{U}_{d} irrep counterpart λ\lambda, and turns out to be flips in the fusion order of the individual tensor factors which decompose into Ud\mathrm{U}_{d} irreps. These flips are implementable in the tensor network representation by F-moves, dubbed F-symbols. In proving that the revised circuit yields the GT basis for Ud\mathrm{U}_{d}, the actions of the Lie algebra generators are covariantly transported through the preparation circuit, the Sn\S_{n} QFTs and the circuits for V†V^{\dagger}, reaching the Ud\mathrm{U}_{d} irrep register and again manipulated by F-moves.

We then move on to constructing explicit quantum circuits for the revised Krovi’s algorithm. It consists of three parts:

  • •

    a pre-processing circuit P\mathrm{P}, which prepares coset states and does an alphabet compression of the ditstrings in the computational basis,

  • •

    quantum Fourier transforms QFTSn\mathrm{QFT}_{\S_{n}}, which perform an irrep decomposition of every representation induced from the trivial irrep of a Young subgroup, and

  • •

    the inverse V†V^{\dagger} composed of the Vλ,μ†V^{\dagger}_{\lambda,\mu} blocks, which puts the multiplicity spaces of the Sn\S_{n} irreps, i.e. the irrep register for Ud\mathrm{U}_{d}, in the correct basis.

Notice that we have removed the Generalized Phase Estimation (GPE) part of the original Krovi’s algorithm, which is unnecessary, as we will show. A comprehensive complexity analysis will yield that the total time and gate complexity are both O~​(n4)\widetilde{O}(n^{4}), dominated by the QFTSn\mathrm{QFT}_{\S_{n}} step, and the space complexity is O~​(n2)\widetilde{O}(n^{2}).

Our time complexity O~​(n4)\widetilde{O}(n^{4}) is the best in literature when d>nd>n. Note that we have removed its polynomial dependency on dd entirely, leaving only polylogarithmic dependence hidden in the O~\widetilde{O} notation. This would facilitate any applications which have a potentially high local dimension dd.

1.4.2. Description of the high-dimensional BCH circuit

Equipped with the pre-processing compression circuit P\mathrm{P}, we explain how to implement the high-dimensional BCH Schur transform. It consists of two parts:

  • •

    a pre-processing circuit P^\hat{\mathrm{P}} adapted from P\mathrm{P}, which does an alphabet compression of the ditstrings in the computational basis,

  • •

    a sequence of nn Clebsch–Gordan transforms of Un\mathrm{U}_{n}

Again, the resulting circuit has a high-dimensional focus, i.e. d>nd>n, and in these cases improves the time complexity of the BCH Schur transform from O~​(d4​n)\widetilde{O}(d^{4}n) to O~​(n5)\widetilde{O}(n^{5}), and space complexity from O~​(d2)\widetilde{O}(d^{2}) to O~​(n2)\widetilde{O}(n^{2}).

2. Preliminaries

In this section, we introduce necessary mathematical background on representation theory and notation. We assume that reader is familiar with basic concepts of algebra, combinatorics, group theory, Lie groups and algebras, and representation theory.

2.1. Schur–Weyl duality

Recall, that Schur–Weyl duality states that the diagonal action ϕ⁡(U):=U⊗n\phi(U):=U^{\otimes n} of the unitary group Ud\mathrm{U}_{d} on the tensor space ℋ:=(ℂd)⊗n\mathcal{H}\vcentcolon=(\mathbb{C}^{d})^{\otimes n} generates a matrix algebra 𝒰nd\mathcal{U}_{n}^{d} that is a commutant of the algebra 𝒜nd\mathcal{A}_{n}^{d} generated by the tensor representation ψ(σ):|x1⟩⊗⋯⊗|xn⟩↦|xσ−1​(1)⟩⊗⋯⊗|xσ−1​(n)⟩\psi(\sigma):\lvert{x_{1}}\rangle\otimes\dots\otimes\lvert{x_{n}}\rangle\mapsto\lvert{x_{\sigma^{-1}(1)}}\rangle\otimes\dots\otimes\lvert{x_{\sigma^{-1}(n)}}\rangle of the symmetric group Sn\S_{n}. Restating this, there exists a Schur transform unitary USchU_{\mathrm{Sch}} that simultaneously decomposes the actions of ϕ\phi and ψ\psi on ℋ\mathcal{H}, viewed as representations of Ud\mathrm{U}_{d} and Sn\S_{n}, into their respective irreducible representations, as follows:

(1) ∀u∈Ud,USchϕ(u)USch†=⨁λ⊢dnIdλ⊗ϕλ(u),∀σ∈Sn,USchψ(σ)USch†=⨁λ⊢dnψλ(σ)⊗Imλ,\begin{split}&\forall u\in\mathrm{U}_{d},\;U_{\mathrm{Sch}}\,\phi(u)\,U_{\mathrm{Sch}}^{\dagger}=\bigoplus_{\lambda\mathbin{\vdash}_{d}n}I_{d_{\lambda}}\otimes\phi_{\lambda}(u),\\ &\forall\sigma\in\S_{n},\;U_{\mathrm{Sch}}\,\psi(\sigma)\,U_{\mathrm{Sch}}^{\dagger}=\bigoplus_{\lambda\mathbin{\vdash}_{d}n}\psi_{\lambda}(\sigma)\otimes I_{m_{\lambda}},\end{split}

where ϕλ:Ud→End⁡(𝒲λ)\phi_{\lambda}:\mathrm{U}_{d}\rightarrow\mathrm{End}(\mathcal{W}_{\lambda}) and ψλ:Sn→End⁡(ℋλ)\psi_{\lambda}:\S_{n}\rightarrow\mathrm{End}(\mathcal{H}_{\lambda}) are irreps of Ud\mathrm{U}_{d} and Sn\S_{n} respectively, with mλ≔dim(𝒲λ)=deg⁡(ϕλ)m_{\lambda}\coloneqq\dim(\mathcal{W}_{\lambda})={\rm deg}(\phi_{\lambda}) and dλ≔dim(ℋλ)=deg⁡(ψλ)d_{\lambda}\coloneqq\dim(\mathcal{H}_{\lambda})={\rm deg}(\psi_{\lambda}), with λ\lambda ranging over all partitions of nn into dd parts, with each partition uniquely corresponding to an irrep of Ud\mathrm{U}_{d} and Sn\S_{n}.

Usually we think of λ\lambda combinatorially as a Young diagram. On the level of vector spaces, we say that ℋ\mathcal{H} decomposes into irreps as

(2) ℋ=⨁λ⊢dnℋλ⊗𝒲λ\mathcal{H}=\bigoplus_{\lambda\mathbin{\vdash}_{d}n}\mathcal{H}_{\lambda}\otimes\mathcal{W}_{\lambda}

with ℋλ\mathcal{H}_{\lambda} an irrep of Sn\S_{n} (Specht module) and 𝒲λ\mathcal{W}_{\lambda} an irrep of Ud\mathrm{U}_{d} (Weyl module). Note that we can equivalently consider representations of GLd\GL_{d} or 𝔤​𝔩d\mathfrak{gl}_{d} instead of Ud\mathrm{U}_{d} since it does not make a difference in the context of Schur–Weyl duality: tensor representations of GLd\GL_{d}, Ud\mathrm{U}_{d} and 𝔤​𝔩d\mathfrak{gl}_{d} generate the same associative matrix algebra on ℋ\mathcal{H}.

2.2. Young–Yamanouchi basis

For irreducible representations of the symmetric group Sn\S_{n}, there are several natural choices of orthonormal bases. A convenient basis for Specht modules is the Young–Yamanouchi basis. It is constructed recursively along the chain of subgroups

(3) S1⊂S2⊂⋯⊂Sn,\S_{1}\subset\S_{2}\subset\cdots\subset\S_{n},

using the branching rule that restricts an irreps of Sk\S_{k} to Sk−1\S_{k-1}. Basis vectors are in bijection with standard Young tableaux of shape λ⊢n\lambda\mathbin{\vdash}n.

Equivalently, basis vectors correspond to Yamanouchi words or paths in the Young graph, which is an example of a Bratteli diagram. For example, a basis label TT can have three equivalent forms:

The action of adjacent transpositions σi=(i,i+1)\sigma_{i}=(i,\,i{+}1) is particularly simple in this basis:

(4) ψλ(σi)|T⟩=1ri​(T)|T⟩+1−1ri​(T)2|T′⟩,\psi_{\lambda}(\sigma_{i})\,\lvert{T}\rangle=\frac{1}{r_{i}(T)}\lvert{T}\rangle+\sqrt{1-\frac{1}{r_{i}(T)^{2}}}\,\lvert{T^{\prime}}\rangle,

where T′T^{\prime} is obtained from TT by swapping ii and i+1i+1 (if T′T^{\prime} is also standard), and ri​(T)r_{i}(T) is the axial distance between ii and i+1i+1 in TT, defined as

(5) ri​(T)=(c⁡(i)−c⁡(i+1))−(r⁡(i)−r⁡(i+1)),r_{i}(T)=(c(i)-c(i+1))-(r(i)-r(i+1)),

with r⁡(j),c⁡(j)r(j),c(j) denoting the row and column of jj in TT. This formula completely determines the Sn\S_{n} action. Sometimes, Young–Yamanouchi basis is also called Gelfand–Tsetlin basis for Sn\S_{n}, but we reserve this name for similar basis of the unitary group Ud\mathrm{U}_{d} and Lie algebra 𝔤​𝔩d\mathfrak{gl}_{d}.

2.3. Gelfand–Tsetlin basis

Irreps of Ud\mathrm{U}_{d} (or equivalently of 𝔤​𝔩d\mathfrak{gl}_{d}) are generally labeled by the highest weights λ=(λ1≥⋯≥λd)\lambda=(\lambda_{1}\geq\cdots\geq\lambda_{d}), which are integers. Similarly to the Specht modules of the symmetric group, the choice of basis for the Weyl modules is also not unique. One such natural choice is the Gelfand–Tsetlin (GT) basis, which is subgroup-adapted to the following chain:

(6) U1⊂U2⊂⋯⊂Ud.\mathrm{U}_{1}\subset\mathrm{U}_{2}\subset\dots\subset\mathrm{U}_{d}.

The GT basis is indexed by triangular arrays (GT patterns)

(7) M={Mk,i∣1≤i≤k≤d},M=\{M_{k,i}\mid 1\leq i\leq k\leq d\},

satisfying the interlacing conditions

(8) Mk+1,i≥Mk,i≥Mk+1,i+1.M_{k+1,i}\geq M_{k,i}\geq M_{k+1,i+1}.

Here the top row Md=(Md,1,…,Md,d)M_{d}=(M_{d,1},\dots,M_{d,d}) equals λ\lambda. Equivalently, GT pattern can represented as Semistandard Young Tableau. For example, here is a GT pattern with top row λ=(3,2,0,0,0)\lambda=(3,2,0,0,0):

(11) wk​(M)\displaystyle w_{k}(M) :=∑i=1kMk,i−∑i=1k−1Mk−1,i\displaystyle\vcentcolon=\sum_{i=1}^{k}M_{k,i}-\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}M_{k-1,i}

2.5. Induction, restriction and Permutation modules

Let GG be a finite group and H⊆GH\subseteq G a subgroup. Suppose ρ:H→End⁡(V)\rho:H\to\End(V) is a representation of HH on a vector space VV. The induced representation ρ~\widetilde{\rho} is the representation of GG on the space

(19) V↑HG:=spanℂ{|ti⟩⊗|v⟩|ti∈G/H,|v⟩∈V},V\Big\uparrow^{G}_{H}\vcentcolon=\spn_{\mathbb{C}}\{\lvert{t_{i}}\rangle\otimes\lvert{v}\rangle\nonscript\>|\allowbreak\nonscript\>\mathopen{}t_{i}\in G/H,\,\lvert{v}\rangle\in V\},

where every group element g∈Gg\in G acts as

(20) ρ~(g)(|ti⟩⊗|v⟩):=|tj⟩⊗ρ(h)|v⟩\widetilde{\rho}(g)\lparen\lvert{t_{i}}\rangle\otimes\lvert{v}\rangle\rparen\vcentcolon=\lvert{t_{j}}\rangle\otimes\rho(h)\lvert{v}\rangle

where we used unique decomposition of g​ti=tj​hgt_{i}=t_{j}h with ti,tj∈G/H,t_{i},\,t_{j}\in G/H, are transversals and h∈Hh\in H (jj and hh depend on ii). In the literature, this induced represention is denoted by ℂ⁡[G]⊗ℂ⁡[H]V\mathbb{C}[G]\otimes_{\mathbb{C}[H]}V. Dimension of the induced representation is |G||H|​dimV\tfrac{\lvert G\rvert}{\lvert H\rvert}\dim\,V.

Consider now a composition μ=(μ1,…,μℓ)\mu=(\mu_{1},\dots,\mu_{\ell}) of nn, and define the Young subgroup

(21) Yμ:=Sμ1×⋯×Sμℓ.Y_{\mu}\vcentcolon=\S_{\mu_{1}}\times\cdots\times\S_{\mu_{\ell}}.

Restriction of an irrep ℋλ\mathcal{H}_{\lambda} of Sn\S_{n} to YμY_{\mu} decomposes as

(22) ℋλ↓SnYμ≅⨁α=(α1,…,αl)αi⊢μiℋα1⊗⋯⊗ℋαl⊗ℂmαλ\mathcal{H}_{\lambda}\Big\downarrow^{S_{n}}_{Y_{\mu}}\,\cong\,\bigoplus_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{l})\\ \alpha_{i}\mathbin{\vdash}\mu_{i}\end{subarray}}\mathcal{H}_{\alpha_{1}}\otimes\dotsb\otimes\mathcal{H}_{\alpha_{l}}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{m^{\lambda}_{\alpha}}

where mαλm^{\lambda}_{\alpha} are multiplicities. For the trivial choice α=((μ1),…,(μℓ))≡triv\alpha=((\mu_{1}),\dots,(\mu_{\ell}))\equiv\mathrm{triv}, this multiplicity is the Kostka number Kλ​μK_{\lambda\mu}.

Conversely, permutation modules are induced representations from trivial irreps of Young subgroups:

(23) 𝒫μ:=triv↑SnYμ≡ℋ(μ1)⊗⋯⊗ℋ(μl)↑SnYμ.\mathcal{P}_{\mu}\vcentcolon=\mathrm{triv}\Big\uparrow^{\S_{n}}_{Y_{\mu}}\equiv\mathcal{H}_{(\mu_{1})}\otimes\dotsb\otimes\mathcal{H}_{(\mu_{l})}\Big\uparrow^{S_{n}}_{Y_{\mu}}.

They admit the decomposition

(24) 𝒫μ≅⨁λ⊢nℋλ⊗ℂKλ​μ,\mathcal{P}_{\mu}\;\cong\;\bigoplus_{\lambda\vdash n}\mathcal{H}_{\lambda}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{K_{\lambda\mu}},

again with multiplicities given by Kostka numbers.

2.6. Clebsch–Gordan transformations

A fundamental structure in the representation theory of groups is the decomposition of tensor products of irreducible representations. Let GG be a compact Lie group (e.g. G=UdG=\mathrm{U}_{d}) and let 𝒲λ,𝒲μ\mathcal{W}_{\lambda},\mathcal{W}_{\mu} denote two irreducible representations (irreps) of GG, labeled by highest weights λ\lambda and μ\mu. The tensor product representation 𝒲λ⊗𝒲μ\mathcal{W}_{\lambda}\otimes\mathcal{W}_{\mu} is generally reducible and decomposes into a direct sum of irreps:

(25) 𝒲λ⊗𝒲μ≅⨁ν𝒲ν⊗ℂcλ,μν,\mathcal{W}_{\lambda}\otimes\mathcal{W}_{\mu}\;\cong\;\bigoplus_{\nu}\mathcal{W}_{\nu}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{c_{\lambda,\mu}^{\nu}},

where the multiplicities cλ,μν∈ℤ⩾0c_{\lambda,\mu}^{\nu}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0} are known as Littlewood–Richardson coefficients. These determine how many times the irrep 𝒲ν\mathcal{W}_{\nu} appears in the tensor product.

A Clebsch–Gordan (CG) transformation is a unitary change of basis implementing the above decomposition. Concretely, it is the isometry

(26) CG:𝒲λ⊗𝒲μ⟶⨁ν𝒲ν⊗ℂcλ,μν.\CG:\mathcal{W}_{\lambda}\otimes\mathcal{W}_{\mu}\;\longrightarrow\;\bigoplus_{\nu}\mathcal{W}_{\nu}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{c_{\lambda,\mu}^{\nu}}.

Relative to fixed bases in the domain and codomain, the entries of CG\CG are called Clebsch–Gordan coefficients. These coefficients resolve the tensor product basis (adapted to 𝒲λ⊗𝒲μ\mathcal{W}_{\lambda}\otimes\mathcal{W}_{\mu}) into a coupled basis, adapted to the irreps 𝒲ν\mathcal{W}_{\nu} in the decomposition.

Special case: SU2\mathrm{SU}_{2}. For the group SU2\mathrm{SU}_{2}, irreps are labeled by spins j∈12​ℤ⩾0j\in\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0}, with dim𝒲j=2​j+1\dim\mathcal{W}_{j}=2j+1. The decomposition simplifies to

(27) 𝒲j1⊗𝒲j2≅⨁j=|j1−j2|j1+j2𝒲j,\mathcal{W}_{j_{1}}\otimes\mathcal{W}_{j_{2}}\;\cong\;\bigoplus_{j=|j_{1}-j_{2}|}^{j_{1}+j_{2}}\mathcal{W}_{j},

where each summand appears with multiplicity one, i.e. cj1,j2j∈{0,1}c_{j_{1},j_{2}}^{j}\in\{0,1\}. The corresponding CG coefficients are exactly the angular momentum coupling coefficients.

Clebsch–Gordan transformation can be thought as being “post-selected” on the output irrep ν\nu and represented in the tensor network notation as follows:

(28)

where i∈[cλ​μν]i\in[c_{\lambda\mu}^{\nu}] is the basis label in the multiplicity space.

In the language of tensor categories, the CG transformation realizes the so-called fusion rules, where the fusion multiplicities coincide with the Littlewood–Richardson coefficients [Sim23]. When we tensor to irreps, we can say that we “fuse” them.

2.7. Split basis

For symmetric groups Sn\S_{n}, one may also work in the split basis, adapted to the restriction to a Young subgroup chain:

(29) Sn⊃Sμ1+⋯+μl−1×Sμl⊃⋯⊃Sμ1×Sμ2×⋯×Sμl≡Yμ,\S_{n}\supset\S_{\mu_{1}+\cdots+\mu_{l-1}}\times\S_{\mu_{l}}\supset\cdots\supset\S_{\mu_{1}}\times\S_{\mu_{2}}\times\cdots\times\S_{\mu_{l}}\equiv Y_{\mu},

where in each individual component Sμk\S_{\mu_{k}} the basis is Young–Yamanouchi. This basis differs from the full Young–Yamanouchi basis, which is adapted to the full chain Sn⊃Sn−1⊃⋯⊃S1\S_{n}\supset\S_{n-1}\supset\cdots\supset\S_{1}. The transformation between these bases can be interpreted as a generalized CG transformation, since it reorganizes permutation modules into irreducible components. This transformation will be of key importance to us, and to describe it later we need to introduce the concept of FF-symbols and FF-moves in the next section.

2.8. Tensor category structures and FF-symbols

The representation categories of both G=UdG=\mathrm{U}_{d} and G=SnG=\S_{n} naturally carry the structure of a tensor category Rep⁡(G)\Rep(G) [Sim23]. Objects are finite-dimensional representations, and the tensor product of representations is again a representation. For irreps 𝒲a,𝒲b\mathcal{W}_{a},\mathcal{W}_{b}, their tensor product decomposes as

(30) 𝒲a⊗𝒲b≅⨁c𝒲c⊗ℂNa​bc,\mathcal{W}_{a}\otimes\mathcal{W}_{b}\;\cong\;\bigoplus_{c}\mathcal{W}_{c}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{N_{ab}^{c}},

where Na​bc∈ℤ⩾0N_{ab}^{c}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0} are the fusion multiplicities. For Sn\S_{n} the Na​bcN_{ab}^{c} are given by Kronecker coefficients, and for Ud\mathrm{U}_{d} they coincide with the same combinatorial rule.

The tensor product is associative, but not strictly associative: when decomposing 𝒲a⊗𝒲b⊗𝒲c\mathcal{W}_{a}\otimes\mathcal{W}_{b}\otimes\mathcal{W}_{c}, one may first fuse (𝒲a⊗𝒲b)(\mathcal{W}_{a}\otimes\mathcal{W}_{b}) and then 𝒲c\mathcal{W}_{c}, or first fuse (𝒲b⊗𝒲c)(\mathcal{W}_{b}\otimes\mathcal{W}_{c}) and then 𝒲a\mathcal{W}_{a}. Each choice yields a (possibly different) orthonormal basis of the same vector space. The change of basis between these two fusion orders is given by a unitary matrix called the FF-symbol:

(31) Fνα​β​γ:⨁δℂNα​βδ⊗ℂNδ​γν⟶⨁θℂNβ​γθ⊗ℂNα​θν.F^{\alpha\beta\gamma}_{\nu}:\bigoplus_{\delta}\mathbb{C}^{N_{\alpha\beta}^{\delta}}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{N_{\delta\gamma}^{\nu}}\;\;\longrightarrow\;\;\bigoplus_{\theta}\mathbb{C}^{N_{\beta\gamma}^{\theta}}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{N_{\alpha\theta}^{\nu}}.

Graphically, FF-symbols implement the recoupling move or FF-move that is, the change of parenthesization (see Fig. 1):

(32) (𝒲a⊗𝒲b)⊗𝒲c≅𝒲a⊗(𝒲b⊗𝒲c).(\mathcal{W}_{a}\otimes\mathcal{W}_{b})\otimes\mathcal{W}_{c}\;\cong\;\mathcal{W}_{a}\otimes(\mathcal{W}_{b}\otimes\mathcal{W}_{c}).

In the case of Rep⁡(U2)\Rep(\mathrm{U}_{2}), the FF-symbols coincide (up to normalization and phase conventions) with the classical Racah WW-coefficients and 6​j6j-symbols. More generally, for semisimple categories like Rep⁡(Ud)\Rep(\mathrm{U}_{d}) or Rep⁡(Sn)\Rep(\S_{n}), the FF-symbols are unitary matrices satisfying the pentagon identity [Mac98], ensuring coherence of associativity.

When multiplicities Na​bc>1N_{ab}^{c}>1 occur, the FF-symbol is not just a number but a block unitary matrix whose indices label the different fusion channels. In many of the cases relevant to Schur–Weyl duality (e.g. when fusing fundamental representations), multiplicities are absent, and FF-symbols reduce to scalar phases or small unitary matrices, see Fig. 1.

In practice, FF-symbols provide the algebraic data needed to manipulate tensor network diagrams built from representation-theoretic building blocks. This makes them a key ingredient in both diagrammatic recoupling theory and computational approaches to representation theory.

3. Two approaches to the Schur transform

In general, the Schur transform is not uniquely defined, as it is specified up to the choice of bases on the unitary and symmetric registers. The most common conventional choice of bases for the Schur transform are the Gelfand–Tsetlin basis and the Young–Yamanouchi basis (together commonly referred to as the Gelfand–Tsetlin bases), which are described in the previous section. However, even for a fixed choice of bases, the approaches to implementing the Schur transform can be fundamentally different. In this section, we describe the main ideas behind two conceptually different approaches to the Schur transform: the BCH approach [BCH06], and Krovi’s approach [Kro19].

3.1. BCH

The main idea behind BCH approach to Schur transform is to treat the full Hilbert space ℋ=(ℂd)⊗n\mathcal{H}=(\mathbb{C}^{d})^{\otimes n} as a tensor product of nn defining irreps of Ud\mathrm{U}_{d} [BCH06]:

(33) ℋ=𝒲□⊗𝒲□⊗…⊗𝒲□.\mathcal{H}=\mathcal{W}_{\square}\otimes\mathcal{W}_{\square}\otimes\dotsc\otimes\mathcal{W}_{\square}.

In that case, we deal with a special case of fusion of irreps, which is called Pieri rule:

(34) 𝒲λ⊗𝒲□≃⨁a∈ACd​(λ)CGd⁡𝒲λ+a,\mathcal{W}_{\lambda}\otimes\mathcal{W}_{\square}\simeq^{\CG_{d}}\bigoplus_{a\in\mathrm{AC}_{d}(\lambda)}\mathcal{W}_{\lambda^{+a}},

where ACd​(λ)\mathrm{AC}_{d}(\lambda) is a set of addable rows of λ\lambda and λ+a\lambda^{+a} is the Young diagram λ\lambda with box added at the row aa. The Clebsch–Gordan transformation CGd\CG_{d} is multiplicity free in this case, which we denote in tensor network notation as

(35)

3.2. Krovi

On the other hand, Krovi’s approach views the full Hilbert space differently [Kro19]:

(36) ℋ=⨁w𝒫w,\mathcal{H}=\bigoplus_{w}\mathcal{P}_{w},

where the direct sum is taken over all possible weights ww of strings x=(x1,…,xn)∈[d]nx=(x_{1},\dotsc,x_{n})\in[d]^{n} (there are (n+d−1d−1)\binom{n+d-1}{d-1} different weights) and

(37) 𝒫w:=spanℂ{ψ(π)|1,…,1⏟w1,2,…,2⏟w2,…,d,…,d⏟wd⟩|π∈Sn}.\mathcal{P}_{w}\vcentcolon=\spn_{\mathbb{C}}\{\,\psi(\pi)\,|\underbrace{1,\dotsc,1}_{w_{1}},\underbrace{2,\dotsc,2}_{w_{2}},\dotsc,\underbrace{d,\dotsc,d}_{w_{d}}\rangle\;\nonscript\>|\allowbreak\nonscript\>\mathopen{}\;\pi\in\S_{n}\,\}.

However, it is clear that different 𝒫w\mathcal{P}_{w} with w=(p,μ)w=(p,\mu) but with the same composition μ\mu are in fact all isomorphic to the permutation module 𝒫μ\mathcal{P}_{\mu}. Recall that pp here is the alphabet map introduced in Section 2.4. So we can write

(38) ℋ=⨁(p,μ)𝒫μ.\mathcal{H}=\bigoplus_{(p,\mu)}\mathcal{P}_{\mu}.

Now recall decomposition of permutation modules:

(39) 𝒫μ=triv↑SnYμ≃⨁λ⊢nHλ⊗ℂKλ,μ,\mathcal{P}_{\mu}=\mathrm{triv}\Big\uparrow^{S_{n}}_{Y_{\mu}}\simeq\bigoplus_{\lambda\mathbin{\vdash}n}H_{\lambda}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{K_{\lambda,\mu}},

where Kλ,μK_{\lambda,\mu} are Kostka numbers. This number is also the dimension of the weight w=(p,μ)w=(p,\mu) subspace inside Weyl module WλW_{\lambda}, and all such weight subspaces comprise the full unitary group irrep λ\lambda:

(40) 𝒲λ=⨁(p,μ)ℂKλ,μ.\mathcal{W}_{\lambda}=\bigoplus_{(p,\mu)}\mathbb{C}^{K_{\lambda,\mu}}.

So, by putting everything together, we get the following decomposition of the full Hilbert space of nn qudits:

(41) ℋ=⨁(p,μ)triv↑YμSn≅⨁(p,μ)⨁λ⊢nℋλ⊗ℂKλ,μ≅⨁λ⊢nℋλ⊗(⨁(p,μ)ℂKλ,μ)=⨁λ⊢nℋλ⊗𝒲λ.\mathcal{H}=\bigoplus_{(p,\mu)}\mathrm{triv}\Big\uparrow^{S_{n}}_{Y_{\mu}}\cong\bigoplus_{(p,\mu)}\bigoplus_{\lambda\mathbin{\vdash}n}\mathcal{H}_{\lambda}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{K_{\lambda,\mu}}\cong\bigoplus_{\lambda\mathbin{\vdash}n}\mathcal{H}_{\lambda}\otimes\big\lparen\bigoplus_{(p,\mu)}\mathbb{C}^{K_{\lambda,\mu}}\big\rparen=\bigoplus_{\lambda\mathbin{\vdash}n}\mathcal{H}_{\lambda}\otimes\mathcal{W}_{\lambda}.

4. Revised Krovi’s Schur transform

Krovi’s original construction of the high-dimensional Schur transform [Kro19, Section 4, Theorem 3] contains two critical issues. The first concerns the final stage of the algorithm. After applying the quantum Fourier transform over Sn\S_{n}, Krovi claims that the subsequent step preparing the unitary register is a classical unitary, i.e., a permutation matrix with entries restricted to {0,1}\{0,1\}. This assumption is incorrect: the required transformation is not a classical gate but rather a genuinely quantum operation. In fact, we show that the correct map is the inverse of a well-defined isometry, which we denote

(42) V=∑λ|λ⟩⟨λ|⊗Vλ=∑λ∑μ|λ⟩⟨λ|⊗|μ⟩⟨μ|⊗Vλ,μ.V=\sum_{\lambda}\lvert{\lambda}\rangle\langle{\lambda}\rvert\otimes V_{\lambda}=\sum_{\lambda}\sum_{\mu}\lvert{\lambda}\rangle\langle{\lambda}\rvert\otimes\lvert{\mu}\rangle\langle{\mu}\rvert\otimes V_{\lambda,\mu}.

This isometry acts blockwise on the multiplicity spaces of Quantum Fourier transform over symmetric group and plays a fundamental role in ensuring the unitarity of the overall transform. The second issue concerns the use of Generalized Phase Estimation (GPE). Although GPE is included as a separate component of Krovi’s circuit, we prove that it is in fact unnecessary: the same information is already encoded by the QFTSn\QFT_{\S_{n}} stage and the isometry VV.

Taken together, these observations allow us to present a corrected and fully consistent version of Krovi’s algorithm. Our revised circuit is shown in Fig. 2, where the isometry VV is made explicit. Crucially, because the state after QFTSn\QFT_{\S_{n}} always lies inside the image of VV, the transformation is reversible. This establishes the corrected version of the high-dimensional quantum Schur transform, which we analyze and implement in detail in the following sections.

Theorem 1 (Corrected version of Krovi’s Schur transform algorithm).

The quantum circuit presented in Fig. 2 performs a (high-dimensional) quantum Schur transform, and implements Gelfand–Tsetlin bases for the symmetric and unitary registers. This algorithm has total gate complexity O~​(n4)\widetilde{O}(n^{4}) and total space complexity O~​(n2)\widetilde{O}(n^{2}) in terms of the number of qudits nn in the input.

Proof.

First, we provide detailed definitions of each operation in Fig. 2 throughout Section 4. Second, we argue in Section 5 that the defined circuit achieves Gelfand–Tsetlin bases for the symmetric and unitary registers. Finally, we discuss implementation of operations P\mathrm{P} and VV isometry in detail in Section 6 and Section 7 respectively. Our analysis shows that the dominating operation is in fact symmetric group QFT with complexity O~​(n4)\widetilde{O}(n^{4}) [KS16]. Therefore, the total gate and depth complexities are O~​(n4)\widetilde{O}(n^{4}), and space complexity is O~​(n2)\widetilde{O}(n^{2}), see Sections 6 and 7. ∎

We now detail each stage—Preprocessing PP, the symmetric-group Fourier transform QFTSn\mathrm{QFT}_{S_{n}}, and the isometry VV; a stage-wise resource summary can be found in Table 1.

4.1. Step 1: Preprocessing

The idea behind preprocessing step is to embed a given qudit string xx into a pair specified by the weight wxw_{x} of xx and transversal element txt_{x} of Sn/Yμ\S_{n}/Y_{\mu}, which sorts xx into increasing order string sws_{w}:

We have the following definitions and properties:

(43) sw\displaystyle s_{w} :=(1,…,1⏟w1,2,…,2⏟w2,…,d,…,d⏟wd)\displaystyle\vcentcolon=(\underbrace{1,\dotsc,1}_{w_{1}},\underbrace{2,\dotsc,2}_{w_{2}},\dotsc,\underbrace{d,\dotsc,d}_{w_{d}})
(44) ψ(tx)|swx⟩\displaystyle\psi(t_{x})\lvert{s_{w_{x}}}\rangle :=|x⟩, i.e. we can think x≡(tx,wx)\displaystyle\vcentcolon=\lvert{x}\rangle,\text{ i.e.\ we can think }x\equiv(t_{x},w_{x})

So we define isometry P\mathrm{P} by the following action:

(45) P|x⟩\displaystyle\mathrm{P}\lvert{x}\rangle :=|wx⟩⊗|txYwx⟩, where |tYμ⟩:=L(t)|Yμ⟩\displaystyle\vcentcolon=\lvert{w_{x}}\rangle\otimes\lvert{t_{x}Y_{w_{x}}}\rangle,\text{ where }\lvert{tY_{\mu}}\rangle\vcentcolon=L(t)\lvert{Y_{\mu}}\rangle
(46) P|sw⟩\displaystyle\mathrm{P}\lvert{s_{w}}\rangle =|w⟩⊗|Yw⟩,\displaystyle=\lvert{w}\rangle\otimes\lvert{Y_{w}}\rangle,

where coset states are elements of the regular representation of Sn\S_{n}:

(47) |Yw⟩:=1|Yw|∑h∈Yw|h⟩=1|Yw|∑h∈YwL(h)|e⟩=1|Yw|∑h∈YwR(h−1)|e⟩=1|Yw|∑h∈YwR(h)|e⟩\lvert{Y_{w}}\rangle\vcentcolon=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\lvert Y_{w}\rvert}}\sum_{h\in Y_{w}}\lvert{h}\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\lvert Y_{w}\rvert}}\sum_{h\in Y_{w}}L(h)\lvert{e}\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\lvert Y_{w}\rvert}}\sum_{h\in Y_{w}}R(h^{-1})\lvert{e}\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\lvert Y_{w}\rvert}}\sum_{h\in Y_{w}}R(h)\lvert{e}\rangle

Note that when you push an action of arbitrary permutation π\pi through P\mathrm{P} then it transforms into left regular action on ℂ​Sn\CS_{n}:

(48) P⋅ψ⁡(π)\displaystyle\mathrm{P}\cdot\psi(\pi) =(I⊗L⁡(π))⋅P.\displaystyle=(I\otimes L(\pi))\cdot\mathrm{P}.

For example, when n=5n=5 then

P:|1,2,1,5,2⟩→|(1,2,5)⏟p,(2,2,1)⏟μ⟩⊗|(23)​(45)⏟t⟩.\mathrm{P}\,:\,\lvert{1,2,1,5,2}\rangle\to|\underbrace{(1,2,5)}_{p},\;\underbrace{(2,2,1)}_{\mu}\rangle\otimes|\underbrace{(23)(45)}_{t}\rangle.

4.2. Step 2: Quantum Fourier Transform over Sn\S_{n}

Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) over Sn\S_{n} is a well known primitive [Bea97]. Recall that

(49) QFT:=∑λ⊢ndλn!∑T,S∈SYT⁡(λ)∑π∈Snψλ(π)S,T|λ,S,T⟩⟨π|=∑λ⊢ndλn!∑π∈Sn(I⊗ψλ(π)⊗Idλ)|λ,Ψλ+⟩⟨π|,\QFT\vcentcolon=\sum_{\lambda\mathbin{\vdash}n}\sqrt{\frac{d_{\lambda}}{n!}}\sum_{T,S\in\mathrm{SYT}(\lambda)}\sum_{\pi\in S_{n}}\psi_{\lambda}(\pi)_{S,T}\lvert{\lambda,S,T}\rangle\langle{\pi}\rvert=\sum_{\lambda\mathbin{\vdash}n}\frac{d_{\lambda}}{\sqrt{n!}}\sum_{\pi\in S_{n}}\lparen I\otimes\psi_{\lambda}(\pi)\otimes I_{d_{\lambda}}\rparen\lvert{\lambda,\Psi^{+}_{\lambda}}\rangle\langle{\pi}\rvert,

where we defined a maximally entangle state Ψλ+\Psi^{+}_{\lambda} in the irrep λ\lambda as

(50) |Ψλ+⟩\displaystyle\lvert{\Psi^{+}_{\lambda}}\rangle :=1dλ∑T∈SYT⁡(λ)|T,T⟩.\displaystyle\vcentcolon=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_{\lambda}}}\sum_{T\in\mathrm{SYT}(\lambda)}\lvert{T,T}\rangle.

This QFT\QFT achieves decomposition of arbitrary linear combinations of permutations, i.e. elements of the group algebra ℂ​Sn\CS_{n} viewed as left and right regular representations, into irreducible components.

It satisfies the following equivariance property:

(51) QFT⋅L(π)=(∑λ⊢n|λ⟩⟨λ|⊗ψλ(π)⊗Idλ)⋅QFT\QFT\cdot L(\pi)=\left\lparen\sum_{\lambda\mathbin{\vdash}n}\lvert{\lambda}\rangle\langle{\lambda}\rvert\otimes\psi_{\lambda}(\pi)\otimes I_{d_{\lambda}}\right\rparen\cdot\QFT

Recently, the complexity of implementation of QFT\QFT was studied in detail [KS16]. Below we present the result without proof.

Lemma 2 ([KS16]).

Quantum Fourier Transform over Sn\S_{n} has total gate and depth complexity O~​(n4)\widetilde{O}(n^{4}). The space complexity is O~​(n2)\widetilde{O}(n^{2}). Moreover, this QFT achieves Young–Yamanouchi basis on both output registers, corresponding to left and right regular actions.

4.3. Step 3: Compression isometry VV

Contrary to Krovi’s claim, the final map from YY-labelled multiplicities to GT multiplicities is not a classical permutation: it’s the inverse of an isometry VV that stitches together split-basis blocks via FF-moves. We define the isometry VV as follows. We can think of VV as being a block matrix:

(52) V=∑λ|λ⟩⟨λ|⊗Vλ=∑λ∑μ|λ⟩⟨λ|⊗|μ⟩⟨μ|⊗Vλ,μ,V=\sum_{\lambda}\lvert{\lambda}\rangle\langle{\lambda}\rvert\otimes V_{\lambda}=\sum_{\lambda}\sum_{\mu}\lvert{\lambda}\rangle\langle{\lambda}\rvert\otimes\lvert{\mu}\rangle\langle{\mu}\rvert\otimes V_{\lambda,\mu},

where domain and range of isometries is Vλ:ℂGT⁡(λ)→ℂSYT⁡(λ)V_{\lambda}\,:\,\mathbb{C}^{\mathrm{GT}(\lambda)}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{\mathrm{SYT}(\lambda)} and Vλ,μ:ℂGT⁡(λ,μ)→ℂSYT⁡(λ)V_{\lambda,\mu}\,:\,\mathbb{C}^{\mathrm{GT}(\lambda,\mu)}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{\mathrm{SYT}(\lambda)}. Matrix elements of Vλ,μV_{\lambda,\mu} are defined for every irrep λ⊢n\lambda\mathbin{\vdash}n, composition μ=(μ1,…,μl)\mu=(\mu_{1},\dotsc,\mu_{l}), map pp, M=(M0,M1,…,Mn)∈GT⁡(λ,(μ,p))M=(M_{0},M_{1},\dotsc,M_{n})\in\mathrm{GT}(\lambda,(\mu,p)) and T=(T0,T1,…,Tn)∈SYT⁡(λ)T=(T_{0},T_{1},\dotsc,T_{n})\in\mathrm{SYT}(\lambda)33 3 We assume T0=M0=()=∅T_{0}=M_{0}=()=\varnothing. as

(53) ⟨T|Vλ,μ|M⟩\displaystyle\langle{T}\rvert V_{\lambda,\mu}\lvert{M}\rangle :=∏k=1l∏j=1μk[FM~k(μk−j),(1),Tj−1k−1](μk−j+1)Tjk−1=∏k=1l((∏j=1μk−1[FM~k(μk−j),(1),Tj−1k−1](μk−j+1)Tjk−1)δTk,M~k),\displaystyle\vcentcolon=\prod_{k=1}^{l}\prod_{j=1}^{\mu_{k}}\left[F^{(\mu_{k}-j),(1),T^{k-1}_{j-1}}_{\widetilde{M}_{k}}\right]^{T^{k-1}_{j}}_{(\mu_{k}-j+1)}=\prod_{k=1}^{l}\left\lparen\left\lparen\prod_{j=1}^{\mu_{k}-1}\left[F^{(\mu_{k}-j),(1),T^{k-1}_{j-1}}_{\widetilde{M}_{k}}\right]^{T^{k-1}_{j}}_{(\mu_{k}-j+1)}\right\rparen\delta_{T^{k},\widetilde{M}_{k}}\right\rparen,

where [Fda,b,c]ef[F^{a,b,c}_{d}]^{f}_{e} are F-symbols or recoupling coefficients44 4 Note, that we have dropped multiplicity indices, see Fig. 1 for a more general FF-symbol., and the convention

(54) Tk\displaystyle T^{k} :=Tμ~k,Tkj:=Tμ~k+j.\displaystyle\vcentcolon=T_{\widetilde{\mu}_{k}},\qquad T^{k}_{j}\vcentcolon=T_{\widetilde{\mu}_{k}+j}.

In the last equality of eq. 53 we have used Tk=Tμkk−1T^{k}=T^{k-1}_{\mu_{k}} and [FM~k∅,□,Tμk−1k−1]□Tμkk−1=δTk,M~k\left[F^{\varnothing,\square,T^{k-1}_{\mu_{k}-1}}_{\widetilde{M}_{k}}\right]^{T^{k-1}_{\mu_{k}}}_{\square}=\delta_{T^{k},\widetilde{M}_{k}}.

The motivation for this definition comes from tensor network contraction and FF-moves, see Fig. 3. Namely, starting from inner product between Young–Yamanouchi basis vector TT and split basis vector M~\widetilde{M} (tensor network on the left in Fig. 3), we get with a sequence of FF moves the diagram on the right, which is trivial.

The fact, that this is the correct definition for the isometry is proven in Section 5, where it is shown that this definition achieves the Gelfand–Tsetlin basis on the unitary group register of revised Krovi Schur transform.

Remark 4.

If μ=(1,1,…,1)\mu=(1,1,\dotsc,1) and p=(1,…,n)p=(1,\dotsc,n), then SSYT MM is actually an SYT. In that case, according to eq. 53, we can easily see that

(56) ⟨T|V|M⟩=δT,M,\langle{T}\rvert V\lvert{M}\rangle=\delta_{T,M},

i.e. the gate VV is classical. Moreover, the state |Yμ⟩=|e⟩\lvert{Y_{\mu}}\rangle=\lvert{e}\rangle and therefore |tYμ⟩=|t⟩\lvert{tY_{\mu}}\rangle=\lvert{t}\rangle. This means that the only non-classical gate inside the Schur transform circuit is QFTSn\mathrm{QFT_{S_{n}}}, which explains an observation that QFTSn\mathrm{QFT_{S_{n}}} can be found as a submatrix inside USchU_{\mathrm{Sch}} when d⩾nd\geqslant n. More formally, our circuit easily explains the following property for the case μ=(1,…,1)\mu=(1,\dots,1):

(57) ⟨λ,T′,M|USch|x⟩=⟨λ,T′,M|QFTSn|t⟩,\langle{\lambda,T^{\prime},M}\rvert U_{\mathrm{Sch}}\lvert{x}\rangle=\langle{\lambda,T^{\prime},M}\rvert\mathrm{QFT_{S_{n}}}\lvert{t}\rangle,

where M∈SYT⁡(λ)M\in\mathrm{SYT}(\lambda) and t∈Sn/Y(1,…,1)t\in S_{n}/Y_{(1,\dotsc,1)} is a transversal which is in one-to-one correspondence with a dit-string x=(x1,…,xn)x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}), i.e. t≡xt\equiv x.

Note that this property is difficult to observe for BCH implementation of the Schur transform.

It turns out that the specific FF-symbols which we need were already computed before, which is the content of the next lemma:

Lemma 5 ([LH87, Eqs. (A9)–(A10)]).

For kk, k′k^{\prime}, λ⊢k′\lambda\,\mathbin{\vdash}\,k^{\prime}, ν⊢k+k′\nu\,\mathbin{\vdash}\,k+k^{\prime} with λ⊂ν\lambda\subset\nu, a∈AC⁡(λ)a\in\mathrm{AC}(\lambda), where aa is a row number of the addable box and λ+a\lambda^{+a} denotes a Young diagram obtained from λ\lambda by adding a box to the row aa,

(58) [Fν(k−1),□,λ](k)λ+a=1k​∏i=1ℓ⁡(ν)(νi−i−λa+a)∏i=1,i≠aℓ⁡(ν)(λi−i−λa+a),[Fν□,(k−1),λ](k)ν−r=1k​∏i=1ℓ⁡(ν)(νr−r−λi+i)∏i=1,i≠rℓ⁡(ν)(νr−r−νi+i)\left[F^{(k-1),\square,\lambda}_{\nu}\right]_{(k)}^{\lambda^{+a}}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{k}\frac{\prod_{i=1}^{\ell(\nu)}\lparen\nu_{i}-i-\lambda_{a}+a\rparen}{\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}i=1,i\neq a\end{subarray}}^{\ell(\nu)}\lparen\lambda_{i}-i-\lambda_{a}+a\rparen}},\quad\left[F^{\square,(k-1),\lambda}_{\nu}\right]_{(k)}^{\nu^{-r}}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{k}\frac{\prod_{i=1}^{\ell(\nu)}\lparen\nu_{r}-r-\lambda_{i}+i\rparen}{\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}i=1,i\neq r\end{subarray}}^{\ell(\nu)}\lparen\nu_{r}-r-\nu_{i}+i\rparen}}

where ℓ⁡(ν)\ell(\nu) is the number of rows in Young diagram ν\nu.

5. Revised Krovi’s approach implements Gelfand–Tsetlin bases for Sn\S_{n} and Ud\mathrm{U}_{d}

In this section, we prove that our corrected version of Krovi’s Schur transform achieves the Gelfand–Tsetlin basis on the unitary register, and the Young–Yamanouchi basis on the symmetric register. For simplicity of notation we treat two registers |p⟩⊗|μ⟩\lvert{p}\rangle\otimes\lvert{\mu}\rangle as one register |w⟩\lvert{w}\rangle. We also define Yw:=Sw1×…×SwdY_{w}\vcentcolon=\S_{w_{1}}\times\dotsc\times\S_{w_{d}}, where if wk=0w_{k}=0 for some kk then we simply omit Swk\S_{w_{k}} from the product.

On the one hand, it is easy to see that an action of permutation π\pi on ℋ\mathcal{H} translates into left regular representation, and therefore after QFT\QFT it acts on the register |S⟩\lvert{S}\rangle, which by construction implements Young–Yamanouchi type action. Therefore, it is trivial in Krovi’s Schur transform that

(59) VQFTPψ(π)P†QFT†V†=∑λ⊢n|λ⟩⟨λ|⊗ψλ(π)⊗Idλ,V\QFT\mathrm{P}\psi(\pi)\mathrm{P}^{\dagger}\QFT^{\dagger}V^{\dagger}=\sum_{\lambda\mathbin{\vdash}n}\lvert{\lambda}\rangle\langle{\lambda}\rvert\otimes\psi_{\lambda}(\pi)\otimes I_{d_{\lambda}},

which basically follows from definitions in Section 4.

On the other hand, to see that the action of Lie algebra generators Ek,l∈𝔤​𝔩dE_{k,l}\in\mathfrak{gl}_{d} is of Gelfand–Tsetlin basis type according to Section 2.3 is completely nontrivial. In the following, we prove directly that tensor representation ϕ\phi of Ek,lE_{k,l} satisfies GT formulas of Section 2.3.

First we define tensor representation ϕ\phi:

(60) ϕ⁡(Ek,l)\displaystyle\phi(E_{k,l}) :=∑i=1nI⊗…⊗I⏟i−1⊗|k⟩⟨l|⊗I⊗…⊗I⏟n−i\displaystyle\vcentcolon=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\underbrace{I\otimes\dotsc\otimes I}_{i-1}\otimes\lvert{k}\rangle\langle{l}\rvert\otimes\underbrace{I\otimes\dotsc\otimes I}_{n-i}

It is obvious that this tensor action ϕ\phi commutes with the tensor representation ψ\psi of permutations:

(61) ϕ⁡(Ek,l)⋅ψ⁡(π)\displaystyle\phi(E_{k,l})\cdot\psi(\pi) =ψ⁡(π)⋅ϕ⁡(Ek,l).\displaystyle=\psi(\pi)\cdot\phi(E_{k,l}).

Consider now the action of QFT\QFT on the coset vector |Yμ⟩\lvert{Y_{\mu}}\rangle:

(62) QFT|Yμ⟩\displaystyle\QFT\lvert{Y_{\mu}}\rangle =QFT1|Yμ|∑h∈YμL(h)|e⟩=1|Yμ|(∑λ⊢n|λ⟩⟨λ|⊗∑h∈Yμψλ(h)⊗Idλ)QFT|e⟩\displaystyle=\QFT\frac{1}{\sqrt{\lvert Y_{\mu}\rvert}}\sum_{h\in Y_{\mu}}L(h)\lvert{e}\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\lvert Y_{\mu}\rvert}}\left\lparen\sum_{\lambda\mathbin{\vdash}n}\lvert{\lambda}\rangle\langle{\lambda}\rvert\otimes\sum_{h\in Y_{\mu}}\psi_{\lambda}(h)\otimes I_{d_{\lambda}}\right\rparen\QFT\lvert{e}\rangle
(63) =∑λ⊢ndλ|Yμ|n!|λ⟩⊗(Πλ,μ⊗I)|Ψλ+⟩=∑λ⊢ndλ|Yμ|n!|λ⟩⊗(I⊗Πλ,μ)|Ψλ+⟩,\displaystyle=\sum_{\lambda\mathbin{\vdash}n}d_{\lambda}\sqrt{\frac{\lvert Y_{\mu}\rvert}{n!}}\lvert{\lambda}\rangle\otimes\lparen\Pi_{\lambda,\mu}\otimes I\rparen\lvert{\Psi^{+}_{\lambda}}\rangle=\sum_{\lambda\mathbin{\vdash}n}d_{\lambda}\sqrt{\frac{\lvert Y_{\mu}\rvert}{n!}}\lvert{\lambda}\rangle\otimes\lparen I\otimes\Pi_{\lambda,\mu}\rparen\lvert{\Psi^{+}_{\lambda}}\rangle,

where

(64) Πμ\displaystyle\Pi_{\mu} :=ΠYμ=1|Yμ|∑h∈Yμh∈ℂ​Sn\displaystyle\vcentcolon=\Pi_{Y_{\mu}}=\frac{1}{\lvert Y_{\mu}\rvert}\sum_{h\in Y_{\mu}}h\in\CS_{n}

In the following, we need to use an important consequence of the Schur’s lemma:

Lemma 6 (Grand orthogonality relations).

For any group GG, its irreps λ,λ′∈G^\lambda,\lambda^{\prime}\in\hat{G} and basis vectors |T⟩,|T′⟩\lvert{T}\rangle,\lvert{T^{\prime}}\rangle the following holds:

(66) 1|G|∑g∈Gψλ(g)|T⟩⟨T′|ψλ′(g−1)=δλ,λ′δT,T′1dλIdλ.\displaystyle\frac{1}{\lvert G\rvert}\sum_{g\in G}\psi_{\lambda}(g)\lvert{T}\rangle\langle{T^{\prime}}\rvert\psi_{\lambda^{\prime}}(g^{-1})=\delta_{\lambda,\lambda^{\prime}}\delta_{T,T^{\prime}}\frac{1}{d_{\lambda}}I_{d_{\lambda}}.

In particular, grand orthogonality relations (Lemma 6) imply

Corollary 7.
(67) ∑λ,λ′|λ⟩⟨λ′|⊗1|G|∑g∈G(ψλ(g)⊗Aλ)|Ψλ+⟩⟨Ψλ′+|(ψλ′(g−1)⊗Bλ′)=∑λ1dλ2|λ⟩⟨λ|⊗Idλ⊗AλBλ.\sum_{\lambda,\lambda^{\prime}}\lvert{\lambda}\rangle\langle{\lambda^{\prime}}\rvert\otimes\frac{1}{\lvert G\rvert}\sum_{g\in G}\lparen\psi_{\lambda}(g)\otimes A_{\lambda}\rparen\lvert{\Psi^{+}_{\lambda}}\rangle\langle{\Psi^{+}_{\lambda^{\prime}}}\rvert\lparen\psi_{\lambda^{\prime}}(g^{-1})\otimes B_{\lambda^{\prime}}\rparen=\sum_{\lambda}\frac{1}{d_{\lambda}^{2}}\lvert{\lambda}\rangle\langle{\lambda}\rvert\otimes I_{d_{\lambda}}\otimes A_{\lambda}B_{\lambda}.

Lemma 9.

For every λ\lambda and ww, we have

6. Quantum circuits for step 1: preprocessing circuits

In this section, we present a quantum circuit for an isometry

(122) P:|x⟩↦|p⟩|μ⟩|tYμ⟩,\mathrm{P}:\lvert{x}\rangle\mapsto\lvert{p}\rangle\lvert{\mu}\rangle\lvert{tY_{\mu}}\rangle,

which transforms arbitrary computational basis vector |x⟩=|x1,…,xn⟩∈ℋdn\lvert{x}\rangle=\lvert{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}}\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{d}^{n} into a triplet (|p⟩,|μ⟩,|tYμ⟩)(\lvert{p}\rangle,\lvert{\mu}\rangle,\lvert{tY_{\mu}}\rangle), where |p⟩=|p1,…,pn⟩∈ℋdn\lvert{p}\rangle=\lvert{p_{1},\ldots,p_{n}}\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{d}^{n} is related alphabet vector, |μ⟩=|μ1,…,μn⟩∈ℋnn\lvert{\mu}\rangle=\lvert{\mu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{n}}\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{n}^{n} is related type vector, and |tYμ⟩∈ℋnn\lvert{tY_{\mu}}\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{n}^{n} related transversal element. To be more specific, recall that the transversal element |tYμ⟩\lvert{tY_{\mu}}\rangle has the following form:

(123) |tYμ⟩=1|Yμ|∑σ∈Sn:xσ⁡(1)⩽⋯⩽xσ⁡(n)|σ⟩.\lvert{tY_{\mu}}\rangle=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{|Y_{\mu}|}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\sigma\in\S_{n}:\\ x_{\sigma(1)}\leqslant\cdots\leqslant x_{\sigma(n)}\end{subarray}}\lvert{\sigma}\rangle.

At first, we shall use the following encoding for any permutation σ∈Sn\sigma\in\S_{n}:

(124) |σ⟩=|σ(1),…,σ(n)⟩∈ℋnn,\lvert{\sigma}\rangle=\lvert{\sigma(1),\ldots,\sigma(n)}\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{n}^{n},

and hence (123) become:

(125) |tYμ⟩=1|Yμ|∑σ∈Sn:xσ⁡(1)⩽⋯⩽xσ⁡(n)|σ(1),…,σ(n)⟩.\lvert{tY_{\mu}}\rangle=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{|Y_{\mu}|}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\sigma\in\S_{n}:\\ x_{\sigma(1)}\leqslant\cdots\leqslant x_{\sigma(n)}\end{subarray}}\lvert{\sigma(1),\ldots,\sigma(n)}\rangle.

Notice that isometry (122), can be defined recursively. Indeed, supposed that we have a transformation:

(126) Prep′:|x′⟩↦|p′⟩|μ′⟩|tYμ′⟩\Prep^{\prime}:\lvert{x^{\prime}}\rangle\mapsto\lvert{p^{\prime}}\rangle\lvert{\mu^{\prime}}\rangle\lvert{tY_{\mu}^{\prime}}\rangle

which transforms computational basis vector |x′⟩=|x1,…,xn−1⟩∈ℋdn−1\lvert{x^{\prime}}\rangle=\lvert{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n-1}}\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{d}^{n-1} into related alphabet vector |p⟩=|p1′,…,pn−1′⟩∈ℋdn−1\lvert{p}\rangle=\lvert{p_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,p_{n-1}^{\prime}}\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{d}^{n-1}, type vector |μ′⟩=|μ1′,…,μn−1′⟩∈ℋnn−1\lvert{\mu^{\prime}}\rangle=\lvert{\mu_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,\mu_{n-1}^{\prime}}\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{n}^{n-1}, and transversal element |tYμ′⟩∈ℋnn−1\lvert{tY_{\mu}^{\prime}}\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{n}^{n-1}. We shall define the following map:

(127) Prepn:|p′⟩|μ′⟩|tYμ′⟩⊗|xn⟩↦|p⟩|μ⟩|tYμ⟩\Prep_{n}:\lvert{p^{\prime}}\rangle\lvert{\mu^{\prime}}\rangle\lvert{tY_{\mu}^{\prime}}\rangle\otimes\lvert{x_{n}}\rangle\mapsto\lvert{p}\rangle\lvert{\mu}\rangle\lvert{tY_{\mu}}\rangle

where |p⟩\lvert{p}\rangle is an alphabet vector, |μ⟩\lvert{\mu}\rangle type vector and |tYμ⟩\lvert{tY_{\mu}}\rangle transversal corresponding to |x⟩=|x′⟩|xn⟩=|x1,…,xn⟩∈ℋdn\lvert{x}\rangle=\lvert{x^{\prime}}\rangle\lvert{x_{n}}\rangle=\lvert{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}}\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{d}^{n}. In that way, transformation (122) can be achieved by

(128) P=Prep1Prep2⋯Prepn\mathrm{P}=\Prep_{1}\Prep_{2}\cdots\Prep_{n}

as presented on Fig. 4. In order to provide a quantum circuit for isometry Prep\Prep, we shall use the above decomposition. Indeed, we will present a quantum circuit for Prepn\Prep_{n}. In that way, the quantum circuit achieving transformation Prep\Prep will be simply given by composing Prepi\Prep_{i} for i∈[n]i\in[n]. Circuits for Prepi\Prep_{i} with i<ni<n are constructed in a completely analogous manner as the circuit for Prepn\Prep_{n}.

In the remaining part of this section, we shall present a quantum circuit for an isometry Prepn\Prep_{n}. We will do it by using two auxiliary registers (|⋅⟩p∈ℋd\lvert{\cdot}\rangle_{p}\in\mathcal{H}_{d} and |⋅⟩u∈ℋ2\lvert{\cdot}\rangle_{u}\in\mathcal{H}_{2}), and further decomposing it into five subroutines (A,B,C,D,EA,B,C,D,E, and FF), see Fig. 5.

We begin with introducing two integer quantities, which will be stored in auxiliary registers. Suppose that |p′⟩|μ⟩|tYμ′⟩\lvert{p^{\prime}}\rangle\lvert{\mu}\rangle\lvert{tY_{\mu}^{\prime}}\rangle are alphabet vector, type vector and transversal corresponding to |x′⟩=|x1,…,xn−1⟩∈ℋdn−1\lvert{x^{\prime}}\rangle=\lvert{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n-1}}\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{d}^{n-1}. For arbitrary |xn⟩\lvert{x_{n}}\rangle, we define a binary number:

(129) cn:={1if ​xn∈{x1,…,xn−1}0otherwisec_{n}:=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }x_{n}\in\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n-1}\}\\ 0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

which is determined by the uniqueness of the value xnx_{n}, i.e., whether value xnx_{n} already appeared in the sequence x1,⋯,xn−1x_{1},\cdots,x_{n-1}. Furthermore, we assign a number en∈[n]e_{n}\in[n]:

(130) en:=i, s.t. ​xn=pie_{n}:=i,\;\text{ s.t. }\;x_{n}=p_{i}

which represents a position of a value xnx_{n} in the sequence p=(p1,⋯,pn)p=(p_{1},\cdots,p_{n}) while sorted ascending.

Subroutine AA. At first, we define unitary

(131) A:|p′⟩|xn⟩|0⟩u|0⟩p↦|p′⟩|xn⟩|cn⟩u|en⟩pA:\lvert{p^{\prime}}\rangle\lvert{x_{n}}\rangle\lvert{0}\rangle_{u}\lvert{0}\rangle_{p}\mapsto\lvert{p^{\prime}}\rangle\lvert{x_{n}}\rangle\lvert{c_{n}}\rangle_{u}\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p}

which computes position ene_{n} and uniqueness cnc_{n} controlled on the registers |p′⟩\lvert{p^{\prime}}\rangle and |en⟩\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle, see Fig. 6(a). In order to compute ene_{n}, we apply a sequence of unitary gates A1,…,An−1A_{1},\ldots,A_{n-1}, where

(132) Ak:|pk′⟩|xn⟩|i⟩p↦{|p′k⟩|xn⟩|i+1⟩pif ​pk′<xn,|p′k⟩|xn⟩|i⟩potherwise,A_{k}:\lvert{p^{\prime}_{k}}\rangle\lvert{x_{n}}\rangle\lvert{i}\rangle_{p}\mapsto\begin{cases}\lvert{p^{\prime}_{k}}\rangle\lvert{x_{n}}\rangle\lvert{i+1}\rangle_{p}&\text{if }p^{\prime}_{k}<x_{n},\\ \lvert{p^{\prime}_{k}}\rangle\lvert{x_{n}}\rangle\lvert{i}\rangle_{p}&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}

which is a controlled XX-gate acting on register |⋅⟩p\lvert{\cdot}\rangle_{p}, see Fig. 6(a). Observe that from (130), we have

(133) A1A2⋯An−1:|p′⟩|xn⟩|0⟩p↦|p′⟩|xn⟩|en⟩pA_{1}A_{2}\cdots A_{n-1}:\lvert{p^{\prime}}\rangle\lvert{x_{n}}\rangle\lvert{0}\rangle_{p}\mapsto\lvert{p^{\prime}}\rangle\lvert{x_{n}}\rangle\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p}

correctly computes the value ene_{n}.

Similarly to (132), we introduce gates

(134) Ak′:|pk′⟩|xn⟩|i⟩c↦{|p′k⟩|xn⟩|i+1⟩cif ​pk′=xn|p′k⟩|xn⟩|i⟩cotherwiseA_{k}^{\prime}:\lvert{p^{\prime}_{k}}\rangle\lvert{x_{n}}\rangle\lvert{i}\rangle_{c}\mapsto\begin{cases}\lvert{p^{\prime}_{k}}\rangle\lvert{x_{n}}\rangle\lvert{i+1}\rangle_{c}&\text{if }p^{\prime}_{k}=x_{n}\\ \lvert{p^{\prime}_{k}}\rangle\lvert{x_{n}}\rangle\lvert{i}\rangle_{c}&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

which is a controlled XX-gate acting on register |⋅⟩c\lvert{\cdot}\rangle_{c}, triggered only if there is an index kk such that pk′=xnp^{\prime}_{k}=x_{n}. Notice that

(135) A1′A2′⋯An−1′:|p′⟩|xn⟩|0⟩u↦|p′⟩|xn⟩|cn⟩uA_{1}^{\prime}A_{2}^{\prime}\cdots A_{n-1}^{\prime}:\lvert{p^{\prime}}\rangle\lvert{x_{n}}\rangle\lvert{0}\rangle_{u}\mapsto\lvert{p^{\prime}}\rangle\lvert{x_{n}}\rangle\lvert{c_{n}}\rangle_{u}

correctly computes the value cnc_{n} written on register |⋅⟩c\lvert{\cdot}\rangle_{c}. Combining (133) and (135), we observe that

A=A1⋯An−1A1′⋯An−1′,A=A_{1}\cdots A_{n-1}A_{1}^{\prime}\cdots A_{n-1}^{\prime},

achieves transformation (131), see Fig. 5 for details.

Subroutine BB. In the following step, we shall update register |p′⟩\lvert{p^{\prime}}\rangle to its new value |p⟩\lvert{p}\rangle in accordance to |xn⟩\lvert{x_{n}}\rangle. We will do it based on the precomputed values ene_{n}, and cnc_{n}. Namely, we will construct the following unitary transformation:

(136) B:|p′⟩|xn⟩|cn⟩u|en⟩p↦|p⟩|cn⟩u|en⟩p.B:\lvert{p^{\prime}}\rangle\lvert{x_{n}}\rangle\lvert{c_{n}}\rangle_{u}\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p}\mapsto\lvert{p}\rangle\lvert{c_{n}}\rangle_{u}\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p}.

Note that |p′⟩∈ℋdn−1\lvert{p^{\prime}}\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{d}^{n-1}, |xn⟩∈ℋd\lvert{x_{n}}\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{d}, and |p⟩∈ℋdn\lvert{p}\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{d}^{n}. Note that depending on the binary value cnc_{n}, we have one of the two cases. If cn=0c_{n}=0, the value xn∉{p1,…,pn−1}x_{n}\not\in\{p_{1},\ldots,p_{n-1}\} is a new value. In that case, we shall swap vector |xn⟩\lvert{x_{n}}\rangle into the right position in the sequence |p1⟩,…,|pn−1⟩\lvert{p_{1}}\rangle,\ldots,\lvert{p_{n-1}}\rangle in accordance to the recomputed value ene_{n}. In order to do it, we introduce the sequence of gates Bn,Bn−1,…,B2B_{n},B_{n-1},\ldots,B_{2}, where

(137) Bk:|pk′⟩|pk−1′⟩|cn⟩u|en⟩p↦{|p′k−1⟩|p′k⟩|cn⟩u|en⟩pif cn=0, and k>n−en,|p′k⟩|p′k−1⟩|cn⟩u|en⟩potherwise,B_{k}:\lvert{p^{\prime}_{k}}\rangle\lvert{p^{\prime}_{k-1}}\rangle\lvert{c_{n}}\rangle_{u}\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p}\mapsto\begin{cases}\lvert{p^{\prime}_{k-1}}\rangle\lvert{p^{\prime}_{k}}\rangle\lvert{c_{n}}\rangle_{u}\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p}&\text{if }c_{n}=0,\text{ and }k>n-e_{n},\\ \lvert{p^{\prime}_{k}}\rangle\lvert{p^{\prime}_{k-1}}\rangle\lvert{c_{n}}\rangle_{u}\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p}&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}

is a controlled SWAP-gate permuting registers |pk′⟩\lvert{p^{\prime}_{k}}\rangle and |pk−1′⟩\lvert{p^{\prime}_{k-1}}\rangle triggered if cn=0c_{n}=0 and k>n−enk>n-e_{n}. Here we use a convention |pn′⟩:=|xn⟩\lvert{p^{\prime}_{n}}\rangle:=\lvert{x_{n}}\rangle, see Fig. 6(b). Notice that unitary operators BkB_{k} do not commute, and are triggered only if cn=0c_{n}=0. Moreover, we have the following:

(138) BnBn−1⋯B2:\displaystyle B_{n}B_{n-1}\cdots B_{2}: |p′⟩|xn⟩|0⟩c|en⟩p↦|p⟩|0⟩c|en⟩p,\displaystyle\lvert{p^{\prime}}\rangle\lvert{x_{n}}\rangle\lvert{0}\rangle_{c}\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p}\mapsto\lvert{p}\rangle\lvert{0}\rangle_{c}\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p},
BnBn−1⋯B2:\displaystyle B_{n}B_{n-1}\cdots B_{2}: |p′⟩|xn⟩|1⟩c|en⟩p↦|p′⟩|xn⟩|1⟩c|en⟩p,\displaystyle\lvert{p^{\prime}}\rangle\lvert{x_{n}}\rangle\lvert{1}\rangle_{c}\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p}\mapsto\lvert{p^{\prime}}\rangle\lvert{x_{n}}\rangle\lvert{1}\rangle_{c}\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p},

which is a desired transformation into |p⟩\lvert{p}\rangle if cn=0c_{n}=0.

In the second case, when cn=1c_{n}=1, the value xn∈{p1′,…,pn−1′}x_{n}\in\{p^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,p^{\prime}_{n-1}\} is not a new value. In that case, we shall uncompute |xn⟩\lvert{x_{n}}\rangle, i.e. |xn⟩↦|0⟩\lvert{x_{n}}\rangle\mapsto\lvert{0}\rangle based on the precomputed value ene_{n}. In order to do it, we introduce the sequence of gates Bk′,Bk−1′,…,B2′B_{k}^{\prime},B_{k-1}^{\prime},\ldots,B_{2}^{\prime}, where

(139) Bk′:|pk′⟩|xn⟩|cn⟩u|en⟩p↦{|p′k⟩|xn−pk′⟩|cn⟩u|en⟩pif cn=1, and k=en,|p′k⟩|xn⟩|cn⟩u|en⟩potherwise,B_{k}^{\prime}:\lvert{p^{\prime}_{k}}\rangle\lvert{x_{n}}\rangle\lvert{c_{n}}\rangle_{u}\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p}\mapsto\begin{cases}\lvert{p^{\prime}_{k}}\rangle\lvert{x_{n}-p_{k}^{\prime}}\rangle\lvert{c_{n}}\rangle_{u}\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p}&\text{if }c_{n}=1,\text{ and }k=e_{n},\\ \lvert{p^{\prime}_{k}}\rangle\lvert{x_{n}}\rangle\lvert{c_{n}}\rangle_{u}\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p}&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}

is a controlled gate acting on |xn⟩\lvert{x_{n}}\rangle by a controlled shift |xn⟩↦|xn−pk′⟩\lvert{x_{n}}\rangle\mapsto\lvert{x_{n}-p^{\prime}_{k}}\rangle if cn=1c_{n}=1 and en=ke_{n}=k, see Fig. 6(b). Notice that in this case, pk′=xnp_{k}^{\prime}=x_{n}, and hence we achieve transformation |xn⟩↦|0⟩\lvert{x_{n}}\rangle\mapsto\lvert{0}\rangle. Moreover, it is easy to see that at most one operator Bk′B_{k}^{\prime} will be triggered, and we have the following:

(140) Bk−1′Bk−2′⋯B1′:\displaystyle B_{k-1}^{\prime}B_{k-2}^{\prime}\cdots B_{1}^{\prime}: |p′⟩|xn⟩|1⟩c|en⟩p↦|p⟩|1⟩c|en⟩p,\displaystyle\lvert{p^{\prime}}\rangle\lvert{x_{n}}\rangle\lvert{1}\rangle_{c}\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p}\mapsto\lvert{p}\rangle\lvert{1}\rangle_{c}\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p},
Bk−1′Bk−2′⋯B0′:\displaystyle B_{k-1}^{\prime}B_{k-2}^{\prime}\cdots B_{0}^{\prime}: |p⟩|0⟩c|en⟩p↦|p⟩|0⟩c|en⟩p,\displaystyle\lvert{p}\rangle\lvert{0}\rangle_{c}\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p}\mapsto\lvert{p}\rangle\lvert{0}\rangle_{c}\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p},

where we observe that |p⟩=|p′⟩|0⟩\lvert{p}\rangle=\lvert{p^{\prime}}\rangle\lvert{0}\rangle for cn=1c_{n}=1. Combining (138) with (140), we observe that

B=Bn−1′Bn−2′⋯B1′BnBn−1⋯B2B=B_{n-1}^{\prime}B_{n-2}^{\prime}\cdots B_{1}^{\prime}\,B_{n}B_{n-1}\cdots B_{2}

achieves transformation (136).

Subroutine CC. Thirdly, we shall update register |μ′⟩\lvert{\mu^{\prime}}\rangle to its new value |μ⟩\lvert{\mu}\rangle, where μ′\mu^{\prime} is a type of a sequence x1,…,xn−1x_{1},\ldots,x_{n-1}, while μ\mu is a type of a sequence x1,…,xnx_{1},\ldots,x_{n}. We will do it based on the precomputed values ene_{n}, and cnc_{n}. Namely, we will construct the following unitary transformation:

(141) C:|cn⟩u|en⟩p|μ′⟩|0⟩↦|cn⟩u|en⟩p|μ⟩.C:\lvert{c_{n}}\rangle_{u}\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p}\lvert{\mu^{\prime}}\rangle\lvert{0}\rangle\mapsto\lvert{c_{n}}\rangle_{u}\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p}\lvert{\mu}\rangle.

Note that |μ′⟩∈ℋnn−1\lvert{\mu^{\prime}}\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{n}^{n-1}, |0⟩∈ℋn\lvert{0}\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{n}, and |μ⟩∈ℋnn\lvert{\mu}\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{n}^{n}. Similarly to construction of the unitary (136), we distinguish two separate cases based on the binary value cnc_{n}. Notice that if cn=0c_{n}=0, the value xn∉{p1,…,pn−1}x_{n}\not\in\{p_{1},\ldots,p_{n-1}\} is a new value, hence, we shall introduce a new element μen=1\mu_{e_{n}}=1 in the sequence μ′=μ1,…,μn−1\mu^{\prime}=\mu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{n-1}. We will achieve it by firstly increasing the value of register |μn⟩=|0⟩\lvert{\mu_{n}}\rangle=\lvert{0}\rangle by one, i.e. |μn⟩=|0⟩↦|1⟩\lvert{\mu_{n}}\rangle=\lvert{0}\rangle\mapsto\lvert{1}\rangle by the following operator:

(142) C0:|cn⟩u|μn⟩↦{|cn⟩u|μn+1⟩if ​cn=0,|cn⟩u|μn⟩otherwise,C_{0}:\lvert{c_{n}}\rangle_{u}\lvert{\mu_{n}}\rangle\mapsto\begin{cases}\lvert{c_{n}}\rangle_{u}\lvert{\mu_{n}+1}\rangle&\text{if }c_{n}=0,\\ \lvert{c_{n}}\rangle_{u}\lvert{\mu_{n}}\rangle&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}

which is a controlled XX-gate acting on |μn⟩\lvert{\mu_{n}}\rangle, and then by applying a sequence of operators Cn,Cn−1,…,C2C_{n},C_{n-1},\ldots,C_{2}, where

(143) Ck:|cn⟩u|en⟩p|μk′⟩|μk−1′⟩↦{|cn⟩u|en⟩p|μ′k−1⟩|μ′k⟩if cn=0, and en>n−k,|cn⟩u|en⟩p|μ′k⟩|μ′k−1⟩otherwise,C_{k}:\lvert{c_{n}}\rangle_{u}\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p}\lvert{\mu^{\prime}_{k}}\rangle\lvert{\mu^{\prime}_{k-1}}\rangle\mapsto\begin{cases}\lvert{c_{n}}\rangle_{u}\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p}\lvert{\mu^{\prime}_{k-1}}\rangle\lvert{\mu^{\prime}_{k}}\rangle&\text{if }c_{n}=0,\text{ and }e_{n}>n-k,\\ \lvert{c_{n}}\rangle_{u}\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p}\lvert{\mu^{\prime}_{k}}\rangle\lvert{\mu^{\prime}_{k-1}}\rangle&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}

is a controlled SWAP-gate permuting registers |μk′⟩\lvert{\mu^{\prime}_{k}}\rangle and |μk−1′⟩\lvert{\mu^{\prime}_{k-1}}\rangle if cn=0c_{n}=0 and en>n−ke_{n}>n-k. Here we use a convenction |μn′⟩=|0⟩\lvert{\mu^{\prime}_{n}}\rangle=\lvert{0}\rangle, see Fig. 6(c). Notice that unitary operators CkC_{k} do not commute, and are triggered only if cn=0c_{n}=0. Moreover, we have the following

(144) C0CnCn−1⋯C2:\displaystyle C_{0}C_{n}C_{n-1}\cdots C_{2}: |0⟩c|en⟩p|μ′⟩|0⟩↦|0⟩c|en⟩p|μ⟩,\displaystyle\lvert{0}\rangle_{c}\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p}\lvert{\mu^{\prime}}\rangle\lvert{0}\rangle\mapsto\lvert{0}\rangle_{c}\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p}\lvert{\mu}\rangle,
C0CnCn−1⋯C2:\displaystyle C_{0}C_{n}C_{n-1}\cdots C_{2}: |1⟩c|en⟩p|μ′⟩|0⟩↦|1⟩c|en⟩p|μ′⟩|0⟩,\displaystyle\lvert{1}\rangle_{c}\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p}\lvert{\mu^{\prime}}\rangle\lvert{0}\rangle\mapsto\lvert{1}\rangle_{c}\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p}\lvert{\mu^{\prime}}\rangle\lvert{0}\rangle,

which is a desired transformation into |μ⟩\lvert{\mu}\rangle if cn=0c_{n}=0.

Furthermore, if cn=1c_{n}=1, we shall simply increase the value of |μen⟩\lvert{\mu_{e_{n}}}\rangle register, i.e. |μen⟩↦|μen+1⟩\lvert{\mu_{e_{n}}}\rangle\mapsto\lvert{\mu_{e_{n}}+1}\rangle. This is achieved by the sequence of gates Cn′,Cn−1′,…,C2′C_{n}^{\prime},C_{n-1}^{\prime},\ldots,C_{2}^{\prime}, where

(145) Ck′:|cn⟩u|en⟩p|μk⟩↦{|cn⟩u|en⟩p|μk+1⟩if cn=1, and en=k,|cn⟩u|en⟩p|μk⟩otherwise,C_{k}^{\prime}:\lvert{c_{n}}\rangle_{u}\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p}\lvert{\mu_{k}}\rangle\mapsto\begin{cases}\lvert{c_{n}}\rangle_{u}\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p}\lvert{\mu_{k}+1}\rangle&\text{if }c_{n}=1,\text{ and }e_{n}=k,\\ \lvert{c_{n}}\rangle_{u}\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p}\lvert{\mu_{k}}\rangle&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}

is a controlled XX-gate acting on register |μk⟩\lvert{\mu_{k}}\rangle, see Fig. 6(c). Note that gates Ck′C_{k}^{\prime} commute, and their order is not important. It is easy to observe that at most one operator Ck′C_{k}^{\prime} will be triggered, and we have the following:

(146) Cn−1′Cn−2′⋯C0′:\displaystyle C_{n-1}^{\prime}C_{n-2}^{\prime}\cdots C_{0}^{\prime}: |1⟩c|en⟩p|μ⟩↦|0⟩c|en⟩p|μ⟩,\displaystyle\lvert{1}\rangle_{c}\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p}\lvert{\mu}\rangle\mapsto\lvert{0}\rangle_{c}\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p}\lvert{\mu}\rangle,
Cn−1′Cn−2′⋯C1′:\displaystyle C_{n-1}^{\prime}C_{n-2}^{\prime}\cdots C_{1}^{\prime}: |1⟩c|en⟩p|μ′⟩|0⟩↦|1⟩c|en⟩p|μ⟩.\displaystyle\lvert{1}\rangle_{c}\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p}\lvert{\mu^{\prime}}\rangle\lvert{0}\rangle\mapsto\lvert{1}\rangle_{c}\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p}\lvert{\mu}\rangle.

Combining (144) with (146), we observe that

C=CnCn−1⋯C2Cn−1′Cn−2′⋯C1′C=C_{n}C_{n-1}\cdots C_{2}\,C_{n-1}^{\prime}C_{n-2}^{\prime}\cdots C_{1}^{\prime}

achieves transformation (141).

Subroutine DD. Fourth, we define unitary

(147) D:|cn⟩u|en⟩p|μ⟩↦|0⟩u|en⟩p|μ⟩D:\lvert{c_{n}}\rangle_{u}\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p}\lvert{\mu}\rangle\mapsto\lvert{0}\rangle_{u}\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p}\lvert{\mu}\rangle

which controlled on the registers |μ⟩\lvert{\mu}\rangle and uncomputes position cnc_{n}, see Fig. 6(d). We can achieve it by applying the sequence of unitary gates Dn,…,D1D_{n},\ldots,D_{1}, where

(148) Dk:|i⟩u|en⟩p|μ⟩↦{|i+1⟩u|en⟩p|μ⟩if en=k, and μk≠1,|cn⟩u|en⟩p|μ⟩otherwise,D_{k}:\lvert{i}\rangle_{u}\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p}\lvert{\mu}\rangle\mapsto\begin{cases}\lvert{i+1}\rangle_{u}\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p}\lvert{\mu}\rangle&\text{if }e_{n}=k,\text{ and }\mu_{k}\neq 1,\\ \lvert{c_{n}}\rangle_{u}\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p}\lvert{\mu}\rangle&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}

which is a controlled XX-gate acting on register |⋅⟩u\lvert{\cdot}\rangle_{u}, see Fig. 6(d). Observe that at most one operator DkD_{k} will be triggered, and only if μen≠0\mu_{e_{n}}\neq 0 which is equivalent to the condition cn=1c_{n}=1. Therefore,

D=DnDn−1⋯D1D=D_{n}D_{n-1}\cdots D_{1}

achieves transformation (147).

Subroutine EE. Fifth, we update the register |tY′⟩\lvert{tY^{\prime}}\rangle to |tY⟩\lvert{tY}\rangle, where |tY′⟩\lvert{tY^{\prime}}\rangle is a transversal of the sequence x1,…,xn−1x_{1},\ldots,x_{n-1} and |tY⟩\lvert{tY}\rangle is a transversal of the sequence x1,…,xnx_{1},\ldots,x_{n}. Indeed, we shall construct unitary:

(149) E:|en⟩p|μ⟩|tY′⟩|0⟩↦|en⟩p|μ⟩|tY⟩,E:\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p}\lvert{\mu}\rangle\lvert{tY^{\prime}}\rangle\lvert{0}\rangle\mapsto\lvert{e_{n}}\rangle_{p}\lvert{\mu}\rangle\lvert{tY}\rangle,

notice that |tY′⟩∈ℋnn−1\lvert{tY^{\prime}}\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{n}^{n-1} is supported on n−1n-1 registers, the last register is initiated in |0⟩∈ℋn\lvert{0}\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{n}, and |tY⟩∈ℋnn\lvert{tY}\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{n}^{n}. Moreover, transversal elements are encoded in the way presented in eq. 125. In order to achieve the above permutation, we shall observe how |tY′⟩|0⟩\lvert{tY^{\prime}}\rangle\lvert{0}\rangle and |tY⟩\lvert{tY}\rangle differs. Notice that if σ∈Sn\sigma\in\S_{n} satisfies condition

(150) xσ⁡(1)⩽⋯⩽xσ⁡(n),x_{\sigma(1)}\leqslant\cdots\leqslant x_{\sigma(n)},

then σ⁡(n)\sigma(n) is equal to one of the following values:

(151) σ⁡(n)=μ~en−1+1,μ~en−1+2,…,μ~en−1+μen\sigma(n)=\widetilde{\mu}_{e_{n}-1}+1,\widetilde{\mu}_{e_{n}-1}+2,\ldots,\widetilde{\mu}_{e_{n}-1}+\mu_{e_{n}}

where μ~k:=∑i=1kμi\widetilde{\mu}_{k}:=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\mu_{i}, and notice that each of the values for σ⁡(n)\sigma(n) appears for exactly the same number of permutations σ∈Sn\sigma\in\S_{n} which satisfy (150). Therefore, we have

(152) ∑σ∈Sn:xσ⁡(1)⩽⋯⩽xσ⁡(n)|σ(n)⟩∝∑ℓ=1μen|μ~en−1+ℓ⟩=∑ℓ=μ~en−1+1μ~en−1+μen|ℓ⟩.\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\sigma\in\S_{n}:\\ x_{\sigma(1)}\leqslant\cdots\leqslant x_{\sigma(n)}\end{subarray}}\lvert{\sigma(n)}\rangle\propto\sum_{\ell=1}^{\mu_{e_{n}}}\lvert{\widetilde{\mu}_{e_{n-1}}+\ell}\rangle=\sum_{\ell=\widetilde{\mu}_{e_{n-1}}+1}^{\widetilde{\mu}_{e_{n-1}}+\mu_{e_{n}}}\lvert{\ell}\rangle.

Moreover, notice that we have the following factorization of elements in transversal vector |tY⟩\lvert{tY}\rangle:

(153) |tY⟩∝∑σ∈Sn:xσ⁡(1)⩽⋯⩽xσ⁡(n)|σ(1),…,σ(n)⟩=∑σ′∈Sn:xσ′​(1)⩽⋯⩽xσ′​(n−1)∑ℓ=μ~en−1+1μ~en−1+μen|σℓ′(1),…,σℓ′(n−1)⟩|ℓ⟩.\lvert{tY}\rangle\propto\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\sigma\in\S_{n}:\\ x_{\sigma(1)}\leqslant\cdots\leqslant x_{\sigma(n)}\end{subarray}}\lvert{\sigma(1),\ldots,\sigma(n)}\rangle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\sigma^{\prime}\in\S_{n}:\\ x_{\sigma^{\prime}(1)}\leqslant\cdots\leqslant x_{\sigma^{\prime}(n-1)}\end{subarray}}\sum_{\ell=\widetilde{\mu}_{e_{n-1}}+1}^{\widetilde{\mu}_{e_{n-1}}+\mu_{e_{n}}}\lvert{\sigma^{\prime}_{\ell}(1),\ldots,\sigma_{\ell}^{\prime}(n-1)}\rangle\lvert{\ell}\rangle.

where

Based on formulas (152) and (153), we shall achieve transformation |tY′⟩|0⟩↦|tY⟩\lvert{tY^{\prime}}\rangle\lvert{0}\rangle\mapsto\lvert{tY}\rangle in two steps. 6.1. Computational complexity

In this section, we argue that the computational complexity of the preparation circuit Prep\Prep is O~​(n3)\widetilde{O}(n^{3}). Firstly, notice that such a circuit is defined recursively as P=Prep1Prep2⋯Prepn\mathrm{P}=\Prep_{1}\Prep_{2}\cdots\Prep_{n}, see eq. 128 and Fig. 4. Hence it is enough to show that Prepn\Prep_{n} has computational complexity O~​(n2)\widetilde{O}(n^{2}).

In fact, the circuit Prepn\Prep_{n} consists of six subroutines A,B,C,D,EA,B,C,D,E and HH, as presented in Fig. 5.

Subroutines A,B,C,DA,B,C,D consist of a linear number of gates Ak,Ak′,Bk,Bk′,Ck,Ck′A_{k},A_{k}^{\prime},B_{k},B_{k}^{\prime},C_{k},C_{k}^{\prime} and DkD_{k}. All of those gates perform a clasical computation, as addition, subtraction, or shift, all controlled on the constant (one or two) number of registers. As such, they can be prepared with O~​(1)\widetilde{O}(1) complexity each. This shows that A,B,C,DA,B,C,D has linear total gate and depth complexity O~​(n)\widetilde{O}(n).

On the other hand, gates EkE_{k} are defined as a sequence Ek=Ek​0⋯Ek​nE_{k}=E_{k0}\cdots E_{kn}, see eq. 157. Each Ek​iE_{ki} defines a controlled Givens rotation, hance can be implemented with O~​(n)\widetilde{O}(n) complexity. Gates Ek′,Ek′′E_{k}^{\prime},E_{k}^{\prime\prime} can be implemented with O~​(1)\widetilde{O}(1) by the same argument in previous paragraph. This shows that EE has quadratic total gate and depth complexity O~​(n2)\widetilde{O}(n^{2}).

Lastly, subroutine HH consists of the SUM subroutine and the linear number of controlled shift gates. From Fig. 9 we see that complexity of the SUM gate is O~​(n)\widetilde{O}(n), which leads to O~​(n)\widetilde{O}(n) complexity of HH.

For completeness, we also note that P uses only constant amount of ancillas in total (since each subroutine is sequential and we can reuse the ancillas), so its space complexity is O⁡(1)O(1).

6.2. Alternative encoding for permutations

In this section, we present an alternative encoding for arbitrary element σ∈Sn\sigma\in\S_{n}, and a quantum circuit subroutine which switches between a standard encoding and the alternative one.

Observe that arbitrary permutation σ∈Sn\sigma\in\S_{n} is uniquely characterized by the sequence (in,…,i2)(i_{n},\ldots,i_{2}) where ik∈ℤki_{k}\in\mathbb{Z}_{k} via following correspondence:

(178) σ=c(1⋯n)in⋅c(1⋯n−1)in−1⋯c(12)i2\sigma=c_{(1\cdots n)}^{i_{n}}\cdot c_{(1\cdots n-1)}^{i_{n-1}}\cdots c_{(12)}^{i_{2}}

where c(1⋯k)c_{(1\cdots k)} denotes a cyclic shift 1→21\rightarrow 2, 2→32\rightarrow 3, …\ldots, k→1k\rightarrow 1. Notice that the number of distinct permutations σ∈Sn\sigma\in\S_{n} coincides with the number of tuples (in,…,i2)(i_{n},\ldots,i_{2}) where ik∈ℤki_{k}\in\mathbb{Z}_{k}.

Consider now arbitrary permutation σ∈Sn\sigma\in\S_{n} determined by numbers σ⁡(1),…,σ⁡(n)\sigma(1),\ldots,\sigma(n). In the following, we present how to determine touple (in,…,i2)(i_{n},\ldots,i_{2}) corresponding to σ\sigma via (178). Firstly, notice that

(179) in=σ⁡(n).i_{n}=\sigma(n).

Secondly, based on the value ini_{n} and permutation σ\sigma, we define the following permutation

(180) σ′:=\displaystyle\sigma^{\prime}:= c(1⋯n)n−inσ=c(1⋯n−1)in−1⋯c(12)i2.\displaystyle c_{(1\cdots n)}^{n-i_{n}}\sigma=c_{(1\cdots n-1)}^{i_{n-1}}\cdots c_{(12)}^{i_{2}}.

Consequtively, based on the form of permutation σ′\sigma^{\prime} in (180), one reads

(181) in−1=σ′​(n−1).i_{n-1}=\sigma^{\prime}(n-1).

Furthermore, based on the value in−1i_{n-1} and permutation σ′\sigma^{\prime}, we define the following permutation

(182) σ′′:=\displaystyle\sigma^{\prime\prime}:= c(1⋯n−1)(n−1)−in−1σ′=c(1⋯n−2)in−2⋯c(12)i2.\displaystyle c_{(1\cdots n-1)}^{(n-1)-i_{n-1}}\sigma^{\prime}=c_{(1\cdots n-2)}^{i_{n-2}}\cdots c_{(12)}^{i_{2}}.

Based on the observations in previous paragraph, we define the following quantum gates:

(183) Gk:|i⟩|j⟩\displaystyle G_{k}:\lvert{i}\rangle\lvert{j}\rangle ↦|i⟩|j+i(mod k)⟩\displaystyle\mapsto\lvert{i}\rangle\lvert{j+i\,(\text{mod }k)}\rangle

where tuple (in,…,i2)(i_{n},\ldots,i_{2}) corresponds to σ\sigma via (178).

Indeed, by applying controlled gate GnG_{n}, see eq. 183, to the last register, we achieve transformation

|σ(1)⟩⋯|σ(n)⟩|0⟩⋯|0⟩|in⟩\displaystyle\lvert{\sigma(1)}\rangle\cdots\lvert{\sigma(n)}\rangle\lvert{0}\rangle\cdots\lvert{0}\rangle\lvert{i_{n}}\rangle
