7. Quantum circuits for step 3: implementation of the isometry VV

In this section, we build a quantum circuit for the isometry VV, defined as in eq. 52 and eq. 53, such that Vλ,μ†V_{\lambda,\mu}^{\dagger} compresses the TT register (elements of which correspond to standard Young tableaux) formed after the QFTSn\mathrm{QFT_{S_{n}}}, into the M~\widetilde{M} register (elements of which correspond to Gelfand–Tsetlin patterns). Recall that this compression is possible because we have a guarantee that our quantum state after QFTSn\mathrm{QFT_{S_{n}}} lies within im⁡(V)\mathrm{im}(V), so the circuit is reversible.

The isometry VV could be implemented recursively using controlled unitaries Fda,b,cF^{a,b,c}_{d}, as shown in Fig. 8. Recall that to convert from GT patterns to SYT, one can describe a transform between the split basis and the Young–Yamanouchi basis, see Fig. 3. Switching between these two different coupling schemes is a change in the fusion order, and as such can be done using FF-moves (see Fig. 1), which are in turn described by FF-symbols. In our case, the FF-symbols take on a special simple form as in eq. 58. Notice that if in [FM~k(μk−j),(1),Tj−1k−1](μk−j+1)Tjk−1\left[F^{(\mu_{k}-j),(1),T^{k-1}_{j-1}}_{\widetilde{M}_{k}}\right]^{T^{k-1}_{j}}_{(\mu_{k}-j+1)} from eq. 53 we treat Tjk−1T_{j}^{k-1} as the output wire of the unitary Fda,b,cF^{a,b,c}_{d}, then it is easy to see that the isometry VV has a recursive structure in TjkT_{j}^{k}, since any FF-move unitary producing Tjk−1T_{j}^{k-1} depends only on the previous entry of the SYT, namely Tj−1k−1T_{j-1}^{k-1}.

M~\widetilde{M} register preparation. In the circuit for isometry VV, the Fl\mathrm{F}_{l} gates are used to prepare (Fl†\mathrm{F}_{l}^{\dagger} to unprepare) the SYT TT in the Young–Yamanouchi basis, using the composition μ\mu and the GT pattern M~\widetilde{M} as control, for l∈{1,…,n}l\in\{1,\dots,n\}. Reading the circuit Fig. 8 from left to right, we first need to prepare the M~\widetilde{M} register to be able to control. We can prepare M~\widetilde{M} using controlled gates on the TT register and the register μ~\widetilde{\mu}. Recall that μ~\widetilde{\mu} is how we denote the register containing the sums of the first kk entries of μ\mu, k∈{1,…,n}k\in\{1,\dots,n\}, that is:

(186) μ~k:=∑t=1kμt.\widetilde{\mu}_{k}:=\sum_{t=1}^{k}\mu_{t}.

It is easy to prepare μ~\widetilde{\mu} from μ\mu using the SUM gate, which takes all μ\mu as input and outputs the sum ∑t=1iμt\sum_{t=1}^{i}\mu_{t} on each wire ii. It is defined in Fig. 9.

In order to then prepare M~\widetilde{M}, we use the property from eq. 53 that Tk:=Tμ~k=M~kT^{k}:=T_{\widetilde{\mu}_{k}}=\widetilde{M}_{k}. It suffices to select these TkT^{k} from the TT register and copy them into the respective places in the M~\widetilde{M} register. To do that, we select using swap gates on the TT register controlled from the μ~\widetilde{\mu} register. This gives the COPY gate preparing M~\widetilde{M}, given in Fig. 11. The controlled swap is defined in Fig. 10.

Main part of the circuit. Now that we have access to M~\widetilde{M}, the main idea to make the control on the Fl\mathrm{F}_{l} gates explicit is to take the pair of composition and step (μ,i)(\mu,i), where i∈[n]i\in[n] is indexing the rows of SYT TT, and convert this pair into the (k,j)(k,j) indices pair, which is labelling TjkT^{k}_{j} from eq. 53 and eq. 54 as well as μk−j\mu_{k}-j and M~k\widetilde{M}_{k}. Here, kk is denoting nonzero rows of μ\mu and jj is defined as:

(187) j=i−∑t=1k−1μt=i−μ~k−1.j=i-\sum_{t=1}^{k-1}\mu_{t}=i-\widetilde{\mu}_{k-1}.
Example 13.

Consider μ=(4,2,1,1,0,0,0,0)\mu=(4,2,1,1,0,0,0,0) for n=8n=8. Then for this μ\mu, to any i∈{1,2,…,8}i\in\{1,2,\dots,8\} we can find a corresponding pair (k,j)(k,j), and in our case the (k,j)(k,j) look like:

i 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8
(k,j) (1,1) (1,2) (1,3) (1,4) (2,1) (2,2) (3,1) (4,1)

We can prepare (k,j)(k,j) from (μ,i)(\mu,i) using the R gate, defined in Fig. 12. Specifically, within the R gate we use the J gate to prepare the (k,j)(k,j) pair from (μ,i)(\mu,i), and we then use the controlled swap and simple algebraic gates to prepare (k,μk−j)(k,\mu_{k}-j) from (k,j)(k,j) controlled on μ\mu. The controlled shift gate is defined as taking the control value and modifying the target value by copying the control and decrementing it by the target entry, as such:

(188) shift:|c⟩|t⟩↦|c⟩|c−t⟩\mathrm{shift}:\lvert{c}\rangle\lvert{t}\rangle\mapsto\lvert{c}\rangle\lvert{c-t}\rangle

The J gate is defined as shown in Fig. 13. We prepare jj by definition, using the ii index register and the μ~\widetilde{\mu} register. Notice that this circuit also uses a constant amount of hidden ancillas for each control, which doesn’t increase the space complexity much.

7.1. Computational complexity

Total gate and time complexity.

First, note that in the VV isometry most of the subroutines are sequential, and we can perform at most a constant amount of gates in parallel. Therefore our time complexity is the same as the total gate complexity.

To implement a given unitary Fl\mathrm{F}_{l}, it is enough to use at most O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) Givens rotations, if we precompute the FF-symbols. Computation of FF-symbols using eq. 58 is clearly very efficient, with complexity polylogarithmic in nn. Therefore, since it is enough to use at most O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) Givens rotations for each FF-unitary and the computation of each FF-symbol is polylog in nn, it should give us the complexity of O~​(n2)\widetilde{O}(n^{2}) to implement one unitary FF.

From Fig. 10 we can determine that complexity of a single controlled SWAP is O⁡(n)O(n). From Fig. 9 we see that complexity of the SUM gate is O~​(n)\widetilde{O}(n). In the implementation of the J gate, given in Fig. 13, the simple algebra gates for control checks each have constant or polylogarithmic complexity in nn, so the total complexity of control checks is O~​(n)\widetilde{O}(n); the X\mathrm{X} gates controlled on μ,i\mu,i each have constant complexity, so the total complexity of controlled X\mathrm{X} gates with the checks is O~​(n)\widetilde{O}(n); two controlled swaps give O⁡(n)O(n), and two SUM gates are O~​(n)\widetilde{O}(n). Therefore the total complexity of the J gate is O~​(n)\widetilde{O}(n). Using this, we deduce that complexity of the R gate is also O~​(n)\widetilde{O}(n).

Therefore, the complexity of one recursive block in Fig. 8, containing two R gates, two controlled swaps, a generalized Pauli X†\mathrm{X}^{\dagger}, and a controlled FF unitary, is O~​(n2)+2​O~​(n)+2​O~​(n)+c​o​n​s​t=O~​(n2)\widetilde{O}(n^{2})+2\widetilde{O}(n)+2\widetilde{O}(n)+const=\widetilde{O}(n^{2}). We have nn of these blocks.

Finally, the complexity of the controlled COPY\mathrm{COPY} gate, shown in Fig. 11, is 2​n​O~​(n)+O~​(n)=O~​(n2)2n\widetilde{O}(n)+\widetilde{O}(n)=\widetilde{O}(n^{2}). With this, the total complexity of VV is given by: 2​O~​(n)+O~​(n2)+n​O~​(n2)=O~​(n3)2\widetilde{O}(n)+\widetilde{O}(n^{2})+n\widetilde{O}(n^{2})=\widetilde{O}(n^{3}).

Space complexity.

The input and output of the circuit for the isometry VV include the μ\mu, M~\widetilde{M}, and TT registers, as well as some constant number of extra inputs of size d=nd=n. We describe the space complexity in terms of the number of wires (states) of size d=nd=n. The registers μ\mu and TT appear before V†V^{\dagger} is executed, but we still describe their space complexity here, for completeness. The register μ\mu is comprised of nn inputs of size nn, so it has complexity O⁡(n)O(n). The register TT is comprised of nn components (plus the 1-dimensional empty set component T0T_{0}) T=(T0,T1,…,Tn)T=(T_{0},T_{1},\dots,T_{n}), where each component TiT_{i} is a partition comprised of (at worst) ii inputs of size nn, giving the complexity of n⁡(n+1)2=O⁡(n2)\frac{n(n+1)}{2}=O(n^{2}) for the register TT. Besides μ\mu and TT, the input to V†V^{\dagger} requires an ancillary register that will turn into M~\widetilde{M} on the output from VV. This register must have the same size as M~\widetilde{M}, and since it is a GT pattern of length nn and entry dimension d=nd=n, we again have nn components with each component Mi~\widetilde{M_{i}} a string of ii inputs of size nn, thus the complexity of M~\widetilde{M} is n⁡(n+1)2=O⁡(n2)\frac{n(n+1)}{2}=O(n^{2}). Therefore, before considering the ancillas needed for the gates, the space complexity from input/output is O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}).

The SUM, controlled SWAP, and (consequently) the COPY gate need no ancillas, so they do not increase the space complexity. After precomputing the FF symbols, controlled FF-unitaries require a constant amount of ancillas, since the Givens rotations require a constant amount of ancillas. Precomputing the FF symbols requires at most O~​(n)\widetilde{O}(n) ancillas to have access to copies of μ,M~k,Tk,λ\mu,\widetilde{M}_{k},T^{k},\lambda, and we can reuse these ancillas after every precomputation, since the FF-unitaries are performed sequentially. Within the R gate, only the J gate requires ancillas. For the J gate, each control needs a constant number of ancillas to do the inequality checks from Fig. 13, but since all the inequality checks are mutually independent we do not need to store any information on the ancilla register between the sequential steps. Therefore, we can refurbish the ancillas after every use (i.e. do control checks, use the ancilla, then reset by inverting the control checks). Thus the J gate only needs a constant number of ancillas. So, in total, we need O~​(n)\widetilde{O}(n) gate ancillas.

Finally, combining the two calculations above implies that the total space complexity of the isometry VV is: O⁡(n2)+O~​(n)=O⁡(n2)O(n^{2})+\widetilde{O}(n)=O(n^{2}).

8. High-dimensional BCH Schur transform

The first approach to the Schur transform, provided by Bacon, Chuang, and Harrow in Ref. [BCH06], is based on sequential applications of the Clebsch–Gordan transforms, see Fig. 15(a). The complexity of this implementation was upper bounded by O~​(n​poly⁡(d))\widetilde{O}(n\poly(d)) in the number of subsystems nn and their local dimension dd, which roughly comes from nn uses of the Clebsch–Gordan transform, each requiring O~​(poly⁡(d))\widetilde{O}(\poly(d)) operations. Recently, this upper bound for Clebsch–Gordan transform was refined to O~​(d4)\widetilde{O}(d^{4}) and for the Schur transform to O~​(d4​n)\widetilde{O}(d^{4}n) [Ngu+24].

In his PhD thesis [Har05], Aram Harrow outlined how to achieve poly⁡(n,log⁡d)\poly(n,\log d) complexity55 5 See the footnote at the beginning of Section 8.1.2 in Ref. [Har05].. Unfortunately, the details of this construction were never fully developed. The key idea is to use a pre-processing compression map that reduces the local dimension of the main part of the circuit from arbitrary dd to d=nd=n, and then apply a sequence of nn Clebsch–Gordan transforms with local dimension nn instead of dd.

In this section, we explore this idea and provide an exact circuit for the pre-processing compression map, which indeed allows one to lift the Schur transform in Ref. [BCH06] to achieve O~​(min⁡(n5,d4​n))\widetilde{O}(\min(n^{5},d^{4}n)) complexity.

The aforementioned key idea by Aram Harrow can be described as follows. A vector x=(x1,…,xn)∈[d]nx=(x_{1},\dotsc,x_{n})\in[d]^{n} of nn symbols, each chosen from dd possible characters, can always be encoded as a vector e=(e1,…,en)∈[n]ne=(e_{1},\dotsc,e_{n})\in[n]^{n} of nn symbols, each chosen from only nn characters, together with an additional decoding vector p=(p1,…,pn)∈[d]np=(p_{1},\dotsc,p_{n})\in[d]^{n}. Formally, the vector x=(x1,…,xn)∈[d]nx=(x_{1},\dotsc,x_{n})\in[d]^{n} is retrieved by

(189) xi=peix_{i}=p_{e_{i}}

for all i∈[n]i\in[n].

As an example, consider the vector x=(9,2,5,9,11,2)∈[11]6x=(9,2,5,9,11,2)\in[11]^{6}. It can be encoded as e=(3,1,2,3,4,1)∈[6]6e=(3,1,2,3,4,1)\in[6]^{6}, together with the decoding vector p=(2,5,9,11,⋅,⋅)∈[11]6p=(2,5,9,11,\cdot,\cdot)\in[11]^{6}, where ⋅∈[11]\cdot\in[11] denotes arbitrary values. Note that the original vector xx can be recovered from ee and pp through (189).

We use this idea and present a quantum circuit for the following isometry

(190) P^:|x⟩↦|p⟩|μ⟩|e⟩,\hat{\mathrm{P}}:\lvert{x}\rangle\mapsto\lvert{p}\rangle\lvert{\mu}\rangle\lvert{e}\rangle,

where |x⟩,|p⟩∈ℋdn\lvert{x}\rangle,\lvert{p}\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{d}^{n}, |μ⟩,|e⟩∈ℋnn\lvert{\mu}\rangle,\lvert{e}\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{n}^{n}, and ee and pp are vectors related to xx by eq. 189. The vector |μ⟩\lvert{\mu}\rangle is the type vector associated with both xx and ee. Such an isometry (190) can in fact be defined recursively. Suppose that we have a transformation:

(191) Prep^′:|x′⟩↦|e′⟩|μ′⟩|p′⟩\widehat{\Prep}^{\prime}:\lvert{x^{\prime}}\rangle\mapsto\lvert{e^{\prime}}\rangle\lvert{\mu^{\prime}}\rangle\lvert{p^{\prime}}\rangle

which transforms computational basis vector |x′⟩=|x1,…,xn−1⟩∈ℋdn−1\lvert{x^{\prime}}\rangle=\lvert{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n-1}}\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{d}^{n-1} into related compressed vector |e′⟩=|e1,…,en−1⟩∈ℋn−1n−1\lvert{e^{\prime}}\rangle=\lvert{e_{1},\ldots,e_{n-1}}\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{n-1}^{n-1}, alphabet vector |p′⟩=|p1′,…,pn−1′⟩∈ℋdn−1\lvert{p^{\prime}}\rangle=\lvert{p_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,p_{n-1}^{\prime}}\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{d}^{n-1}, type vector |μ′⟩=|μ1′,…,μn−1′⟩∈ℋnn−1\lvert{\mu^{\prime}}\rangle=\lvert{\mu_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,\mu_{n-1}^{\prime}}\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{n}^{n-1}. We shall define the following map:

(192) Prep^n:|e′⟩|μ′⟩|p′⟩⊗|xn⟩↦|e⟩|μ⟩|p⟩.\widehat{\Prep}_{n}:\lvert{e^{\prime}}\rangle\lvert{\mu^{\prime}}\rangle\lvert{p^{\prime}}\rangle\otimes\lvert{x_{n}}\rangle\mapsto\lvert{e}\rangle\lvert{\mu}\rangle\lvert{p}\rangle.

In that way, transformation (190) can be achieved by

(193) P^=Prep^1Prep^2⋯Prep^n\hat{\mathrm{P}}=\widehat{\Prep}_{1}\widehat{\Prep}_{2}\cdots\widehat{\Prep}_{n}

as presented on Fig. 14(a).

In fact, a circuit for Prep^n\widehat{\Prep}_{n} can be directly composed from the subroutines A,B,C,A,B,C, and DD presented in Section 6 (see Fig. 14(b)). According to the analysis of computational complexity in Section 6.1, the subroutines A,B,C,DA,B,C,D each have linear total gate and time complexity O~​(n)\widetilde{O}(n). As a result, the computational complexity of the preparation circuit P^\hat{\mathrm{P}} is O~​(n2)\widetilde{O}(n^{2}), since it is recursively defined via eq. 193. It also requires linear number O~​(n)\widetilde{O}(n) of ancillas.

In the following part of this section, we explain how the preparation circuit P^\hat{\mathrm{P}} lifts the computational complexity of the Schur transform from O~​(d4​n)\widetilde{O}(d^{4}n) to O~​(min⁡(n5,d4​n))\widetilde{O}(\min(n^{5},d^{4}n)), building on the original approach of Bacon, Chuang, and Harrow in Ref. [BCH06].

The quantum circuit for the Schur transform in Ref. [BCH06] is based on sequential applications of the Clebsch–Gordan transform. Fig. 15(a) present this circuit, which consists of nn successive Clebsch–Gordan transforms. We refer to [BCH06] and the more recent works [Ngu23, GBO23a] for details. Since the dd-dimensional Clebsch–Gordan transform can be implemented with complexity O~​(d4)\widetilde{O}(d^{4}), the overall complexity of this version of the Schur transform is O~​(n​d4)\widetilde{O}(nd^{4}). It is worth noting that, depending on the encoding of Gelfand–Tsetlin patterns, the space requirements are O~​(d​(n+d))\widetilde{O}(d(n+d)) for the standard encoding and O~​(d2)\widetilde{O}(d^{2}) for the more efficient Yamanouchi encoding; see Refs. [Ngu23, GBO23a] for details. A sketch of the circuit is shown in Fig. 15(a).

The key idea, originally outlined by Aram Harrow [Har05], is to compress an arbitrary vector |x⟩∈[d]n\lvert{x}\rangle\in[d]^{n} into e=(e1,…,en)∈[n]ne=(e_{1},\dotsc,e_{n})\in[n]^{n} and then apply a sequence of nn-dimensional Clebsch–Gordan transforms to ee, as illustrated in Fig. 15(b). Since the preparation circuit can be implemented with space complexity O~​(n2)\widetilde{O}(n^{2}) and each nn-dimensional Clebsch–Gordan transform requires O~​(n4)\widetilde{O}(n^{4}) gates and depth, the overall gate and time complexity of this enhanced version of the Schur transform is O~​(min⁡(n5,n​d4))\widetilde{O}(\min(n^{5},nd^{4})). For simplicity, Fig. 15 sketches the circuit only for the more efficient Yamanouchi encoding. As final step in out argument, in the next section we describe why replacing CGd\CG_{d} transform by CGn\CG_{n} does not break the correctness of the circuit.

8.1. Reduced Wigner unitary

In this section, we explain why our high-dimensional circuit implements the same Schur transform unitary as the original BCH Schur transform.

The reason for that is the building blocks of Clebsch–Gordan transform are so-called Reduced Wigner unitaries RWdλ,ν\mathrm{RW}^{\lambda,\nu}_{d}, which have matrix entries that do not depend to the local dimension, once d⩾nd\geqslant n. To see that, we recall from [VK92] that matrix entries of RWd\mathrm{RW}_{d} for j∈{0,1,…,d−1}j\in\{0,1,\dotsc,d-1\}, i∈{1,…,d}i\in\{1,\dotsc,d\} are (see also Fig. 17)

⟨i|RWdMd,Nd−1|j⟩\displaystyle\langle{i}\rvert\mathrm{RW}_{d}^{M_{d},N_{d-1}}\lvert{j}\rangle ={S⁡(i,j)​|∏k≠j(ℓk,d−1−ℓi,d−1)​∏k≠i(ℓk,d−ℓj,d−1)∏k≠i(ℓk,d−ℓi,d)​∏k≠j(ℓk,d−1−ℓj,d−1−1)|1/2, if ​j∈{1,…,d−1}|∏k=1d−1(ℓk,d−1−ℓi,d−1)∏k≠i(ℓk,d−ℓi,d)|1/2, if ​j=0\displaystyle=\begin{cases}S(i,j)\left|\frac{\prod_{k\neq j}\left(\ell_{k,d-1}-\ell_{i,d}-1\right)\prod_{k\neq i}\left(\ell_{k,d}-\ell_{j,d-1}\right)}{\prod_{k\neq i}\left(\ell_{k,d}-\ell_{i,d}\right)\prod_{k\neq j}\left(\ell_{k,d-1}-\ell_{j,d-1}-1\right)}\right|^{1/2},&\text{ if }j\in\{1,\dotsc,d-1\}\\ \left|\frac{\prod_{k=1}^{d-1}\left(\ell_{k,d-1}-\ell_{i,d}-1\right)}{\prod_{k\neq i}\left(\ell_{k,d}-\ell_{i,d}\right)}\right|^{1/2},&\text{ if }j=0\end{cases}

where

ℓk,d\displaystyle\ell_{k,d} :=Mkd−k,ℓk,d−1:=Nkd−1−k−δk,jS(i,j):={1 if ​i⩽j−1 if ​i>j.\displaystyle\vcentcolon=M^{d}_{k}-k,\quad\quad\ell_{k,d-1}\vcentcolon=N^{d-1}_{k}-k-\delta_{k,j}\quad\quad S(i,j)\vcentcolon=\begin{cases}1&\text{ if }i\leqslant j\\ -1&\text{ if }i>j.\end{cases}

From these formulas we directly see, that the ratios under square roots do not depend on the actual local dimension, but rather on the shape of Yound diagrams MdM_{d} and Nd−1N_{d-1}. Therefore, when multiplying RW\mathrm{RW} unitaries in Fig. 16, the resulting transformation will only depend on the Young diagram shapes which correspond to the rows of the Gelfand–Tsetlin pattern and not on how many zeros are padded to the right in any given row.
